_meta.title: Watoto Playable Content Library

designTiers.parent-led: Ages 0-2: cozy, slow, real-world; parent is primary user.
designTiers.encourage-effort: Ages 3-5: friendly narrator rewards effort, never time pressure.
designTiers.gamify-gently: Ages 6-7: badges & levels, clear repeatable instructions.

universalRules: No timers / no time pressure on any item (timed=false everywhere).
Offline-playable; all assets are local refs.
Captions for all narration; adjustable speed; diverse representation.

stages.title: Sensory & Cause-and-Effect
stages.focus: Sensory-motor foundations rather than school subjects. Zero reading.

stages.title: First Words & Concepts
stages.focus: Build vocabulary and begin categorizing the world. Single-tap, no text.

stages.title: Language Explosion & Early Logic
stages.focus: Vocabulary booms; symbolic and pretend play emerge. One word / emoji max.

stages.title: Pre-Literacy & Foundational Math
stages.focus: Groundwork for reading, writing and arithmetic through play. Reward effort.

stages.title: Early Reading & Number Sense
stages.focus: Kindergarten-readiness skills, still delivered through play.

stages.title: Kindergarten: Foundations in Academic Subjects
stages.focus: More structured learning with hands-on, colorful activities. Gentle gamification.

stages.title: Grade 1: Fluency & Deeper Understanding
stages.focus: Reading fluency takes off; math grows more abstract. Badges and levels.

stages.title: Grade 2: Expanding Knowledge & Skills
stages.focus: More independent learners; longer, richer interactive lessons. Growing autonomy.

stages.title: Grade 3: Critical Thinking & Independence
stages.focus: Shift from learning-to-read to reading-to-learn; more abstract math.

stages.title: Grade 4: Abstract Thinking & Synthesis
stages.focus: Abstract reasoning, multi-step problems, technology to create.

content.subject: Social-Emotional
content.title: Calm-Down Breathing

steps.narration: Breathe in as the balloon grows. Hold...

steps.narration: Breathe out as the balloon shrinks. Aaah.
steps.feedback: Calm chime. 'You did it. Feel calmer?'

steps.feedback: Slower than the first one. Well done.

steps.narration: You have a tool now, and it goes everywhere with you.

content.subject: Math

steps.feedback: '3 and 2 is 5!'

steps.narration: 5 and 0 make 5 too. Drag the empty box across.
steps.feedback: '5 and nothing is still 5!'

steps.narration: I have 2. How many more to make 5?
steps.feedback: 3! You worked backwards to find it.

steps.narration: How many different pairs make 5? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Several! 4+1, 3+2, 5+0 — all the same total.

steps.narration: Five can be split up lots of ways.

3 and 2 make…

content.subject: Math
content.title: More, Less, Equal
content.objective: Compare two groups.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Which has more? Tap the bigger group.
steps.feedback: 'That group has more!'

steps.narration: These two are the same. They are equal.
steps.feedback: 'Equal. The same number!'

steps.narration: Which group has fewer? Tap the smaller one.
steps.feedback: 'Fewer. That group is smaller!'

steps.narration: How could you make the two groups equal? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Add one to the small side, or take one off the big.

steps.narration: Now compare these two. More, less, or equal? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Counting both is how you know for sure.

steps.narration: More, less and equal are how numbers get compared.

The group with the bigger number has…

content.subject: Math

steps.narration: Lay the cubes along the pencil. How long is it?
steps.feedback: Four cubes long! You measured end to end.

steps.narration: The crayon is shorter. Three cubes.
steps.feedback: 'Three cubes. Shorter!'

steps.narration: Measure the book. How many cubes long?
steps.feedback: Six cubes! Line them up end to end.

steps.narration: What happens if you leave a gap between cubes? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: The answer comes out wrong. No gaps!

steps.narration: Which is longer: the pencil or the crayon? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: The pencil — four cubes against three.

steps.narration: Measuring is counting, laid end to end.
steps.feedback: Careful lining up is the whole skill.

Which was shorter?

content.subject: Reading & Writing
content.title: Blend the Sounds: c-a-t
content.objective: Blend three sounds into a CVC word.

steps.narration: Tap each sound: /c/ ... /a/ ... /t/.
steps.feedback: Each letter lights up and says its sound.

steps.narration: Now slide them together: c-a-t.
steps.feedback: 'cat!' A cat appears and meows. Great blending!

steps.narration: Now try h-a-t. Tap each sound.
steps.feedback: /h/ ... /a/ ... /t/. Three sounds.

steps.narration: What word do those three sounds make? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: 'hat!' You blended it yourself.

steps.narration: Change the /h/ to /c/. What word now? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: 'cat!' One sound changed the whole word.

steps.narration: You read two words by blending, not guessing.
steps.feedback: That is really reading.

steps.feedback: 'the'. A word we see a lot!

steps.narration: Now tap the word 'I'.
steps.feedback: 'I'. That means you!

steps.feedback: 'a'. One letter, a whole word!

steps.narration: Find 'the' in this line.
steps.feedback: There it is. Sight words show up everywhere.

steps.narration: Which of these is NOT a sight word you know? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Right. You know the other three by sight now.

steps.narration: Some words you sound out; some you just know.

content.subject: Reading & Writing
content.title: Write Your Letters

assets.desc: Letters a and b to trace

steps.narration: Trace the letter a. Start at the top.
steps.feedback: Nice. That's an a!

steps.narration: Now trace the letter b.
steps.feedback: You wrote a b! Great writing.

steps.narration: Now trace the letter c. One curve, no lifting.
steps.feedback: A single smooth curve. That is a c!

steps.narration: Trace a, then c. They start the same way.
steps.feedback: Same curve, different ending!

steps.narration: Write the first letter of your own name.
steps.feedback: Your letter, in your own hand.

steps.narration: Letters are made of curves and lines you can already draw.
steps.feedback: Writing is drawing that everyone can read.

content.subject: Reading & Writing
content.title: Blend Words
content.objective: Blend three sounds into a word.

steps.narration: Sound it out: d-o-g. Tap to blend.

steps.narration: Now m-a-p.
steps.feedback: 'map!' Well blended.

steps.narration: Sound it out: s-u-n. Tap your answer.

steps.narration: Now b-u-s. Take your time. Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: 'bus!' Slow blending is still blending.

steps.narration: Which word has the /o/ sound in the middle? Tap your answer.

steps.narration: Four words blended today, none of them guessed.
steps.feedback: Slow and right beats fast and wrong.

recap.prompt: Blend d-o-g. What word is it?
Blend m-a-p. What word is it?

content.subject: Reading & Writing
content.title: Word Family: -ig
content.objective: Read words in the -ig family.

steps.narration: p + ig = pig. Tap to read.
steps.feedback: 'pig!'

steps.narration: b + ig = big. d + ig = dig.
steps.feedback: 'big! dig!' Same ending sound.

steps.narration: f + ig = ? Sound it out. Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: 'fig!' Same ending, new beginning.

steps.narration: Which of these is NOT in the -ig family? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Right — it ends with a different sound.

steps.narration: Make up your own -ig word, even a silly one. Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: If it rhymes, the family accepts it!

steps.narration: Learn one family and you can read all of it.
steps.feedback: That is why word families are worth knowing.

recap.prompt: p + ig makes which word?
Which ending sound do pig, big and dig share?

content.subject: Reading & Writing

steps.feedback: 'see'. Every sentence has a doing word.

steps.narration: What is at the end of every sentence? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: A full stop. It tells you where to breathe.

steps.narration: You read three whole sentences today.
steps.feedback: Letters, then words, and now sentences. That is the ladder.

steps.feedback: Living! It grows and drinks, even without moving.

steps.feedback: No. Moving is not enough — it must grow and eat.

content.subject: Health
content.title: Wash Your Hands

steps.narration: Germs are living things far too small to see. They can sit on your hands.

steps.feedback: Germs hide in the places we rush past.

steps.feedback: Soap and water together. That is the pair that cleans.

steps.narration: You have been playing outside in the dirt. What now?
steps.feedback: Wash your hands. Before you touch food or your face.

steps.narration: Last step: dry with a clean cloth. Wet hands pick germs up again.
steps.feedback: Clean, scrubbed, dry.

steps.narration: You know the whole routine now.
steps.feedback: Wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry. Every time.

steps.feedback: Sleep is not lost time. It is when learning sticks.

steps.narration: A book before bed is calmer than a bright screen. Tap the book.
steps.feedback: A story slows you down. A screen wakes you up.

steps.narration: Teeth get brushed before bed, every night. Tap the brush.
steps.feedback: Same order every night is what makes it easy.

steps.narration: Which helps you sleep: a quiet book or a bright screen? Tap the book.
steps.feedback: The book. Bright light keeps your brain awake.

steps.narration: Same steps, same time, every night.
steps.feedback: A bedtime routine is a gift to tomorrow's you.

What helps us sleep well?

steps.narration: Watch: a helmet and a seatbelt do the same job — they hold you still.

steps.narration: Helmet on, seatbelt clicked, both ways looked.

What should you do in a car?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Add and Subtract Within 20
content.objective: Add and subtract using a number line.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 8 + 5: start at 8 and hop forward 5.
Now 13 - 4: hop backward 4.
steps.feedback: Land on 9. 13 - 4 = 9. Nice!

steps.narration: Now 9 + 6: start at 9 and hop forward 6.
Watch the shortcut: 9 + 6 is 10 + 5, because one hops over.
steps.feedback: Making ten first is faster than counting every hop.

steps.narration: Use the shortcut: 8 + 7. Make ten first.
steps.feedback: 15! 8 + 2 is 10, then 5 more.

steps.narration: Now backward: 16 - 7. Hop back from 16.
steps.feedback: 9! Subtraction hops the other way.

steps.narration: You have 12 coins and spend 5. How many are left?
steps.feedback: 7! The number line works on money too.

steps.narration: Forward to add, backward to subtract, all the way to 20.
steps.feedback: One number line, both operations.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Add to 20
content.objective: Add numbers within twenty.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Big sums can be easy. Watch this one: 8 + 7.
steps.feedback: Let's find a trick.

steps.narration: Ten is our friend. It is easy to add to ten.
steps.feedback: So let's make a ten first.

steps.narration: Eight is nearly ten. How much more does it need? 8 + ? = 10.
steps.feedback: That's it. 8 + 2 = 10.

steps.narration: We borrowed that 2 from the 7. Now take it away: 7 - 2.
steps.feedback: Let's see how much is left.

steps.narration: 7 - 2. Seven, give away two.
steps.feedback: 5 is left.

steps.narration: Now the hard sum has become an easy one: 10 + 5.
steps.feedback: 10 and 5 is 15!

steps.narration: So 8 + 7 = 15. Making ten turned a hard sum into an easy one.
steps.feedback: That trick works every time.

steps.narration: Your turn. We want to add 9 + 6.
steps.feedback: Right. 9 needs just 1 more.
steps.prompt: What does 9 need to make ten?

steps.narration: Take 1 from the 6 to make ten, then add what is left.
steps.feedback: 10 and 5 is 15. You did it the clever way!

steps.narration: Last one, all by yourself: 7 + 5.
steps.feedback: 12! Making ten works every single time.

recap.prompt: Which trick helped you add 8 + 7?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Subtract to 20
content.objective: Subtract within twenty.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Taking away can use the same ten trick. Try 15 − 7.
steps.feedback: Watch how we do it.

steps.narration: Instead of taking all 7 at once, we step down to ten first.
steps.feedback: Ten is an easy place to stand.

steps.narration: How far is 15 from 10?
steps.feedback: 5 steps down.

steps.narration: We have taken 5 of the 7 away. Two more still to go.
steps.feedback: 7 is 5 and 2.

steps.narration: Take the last 2 from our ten.
Down to ten, then down again. That is the whole trick.
steps.feedback: Now you try some.

steps.narration: This one lands on ten in a single step.
steps.feedback: 16 − 6 = 10. Straight to ten!

steps.narration: 14 − 5. Step down to ten, then take what is left.
steps.feedback: 9! Four to reach ten, then one more.

steps.narration: One more on your own: 13 − 4.
steps.feedback: 9! You are subtracting like a mathematician.

recap.prompt: Which trick helped you subtract?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Tens and Ones to 99
content.objective: Read two-digit numbers.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Big numbers are made of tens and ones. Look at 47.
steps.feedback: Two digits, two jobs.

steps.narration: The 4 is not really four. It means four bundles of ten: 40.
steps.feedback: Where a digit stands changes what it is worth.

steps.narration: Count the bundles of ten in 47.
steps.feedback: Four tens. That is 40.

steps.narration: The loose ones are the leftovers that could not make a bundle.
steps.feedback: 7 ones. So 47 is 40 and 7.

steps.narration: Say it out loud: forty… seven. The number tells you its own parts.
steps.feedback: Every two-digit number works this way.

steps.narration: Now backwards: build the number from its parts.
steps.feedback: 6 tens and 2 ones is 62.
steps.prompt: Which number has 6 tens and 2 ones?

steps.narration: Careful with this one. There are no loose ones at all.
steps.feedback: 80. A zero holds the ones place open.

steps.narration: Tens are worth more than ones, so look at the tens first.
steps.feedback: 85 has 8 tens; 58 has only 5.

steps.narration: Last one: build 5 tens and 9 ones.
steps.feedback: 59! You can read any number now.

recap.prompt: In the number 47, how many tens?
In the number 47, how many ones?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Tell Time to the Hour
content.objective: Read a clock at o'clock.
content.parentNote: Point out o'clock times on a real clock together.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: The big hand is on 12, the little hand on 3. That's 3 o'clock. Tap 3 o'clock.
steps.feedback: '3 o'clock!'

steps.narration: When the big hand points up to 12, we say 'o'clock'.
steps.feedback: You can tell time!

steps.narration: Little hand on 7, big hand on 12. Tap 7 o'clock.
steps.feedback: 7 o'clock. The little hand names the hour.

steps.narration: Watch: the big hand goes all the way round while the little one moves one number.
steps.feedback: That whole trip is one hour.

steps.narration: Set the clock to 9 o'clock. Tap the 9.
steps.feedback: 9 o'clock. Big hand up, little hand on 9.

steps.narration: School starts at 8 o'clock. Tap the clock that shows it.
steps.feedback: You read a real time off a real clock.

steps.narration: The little hand is on 4 and the big hand on 12. What hour is it?
steps.feedback: 4! Little hand for the hour, every time.

steps.narration: Big hand on 12 means o'clock, and the little hand says which.
steps.feedback: You can read the clock on the wall now.

recap.prompt: The big hand pointing to 12 means…
Little hand on 3, big hand on 12. What time is it?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Coins and Money
content.objective: Recognize coins and their value.
content.parentNote: Sort and count coins together (use your local currency).
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Coins are small, but each one is worth a different amount.
steps.feedback: Size does not tell you the value. The number does.

steps.narration: Read the number on each coin.
steps.feedback: 10 is worth more than 5, even if the coin looks smaller.
steps.prompt: Which is worth more, a 5 or a 10?

steps.narration: Tap each coin in the pile to count them.
steps.feedback: Three coins, but we still do not know how much money that is.

steps.narration: Counting coins is not the same as counting money.
steps.feedback: To find the money, add the values.

steps.narration: Two coins marked 5.
steps.feedback: 10! Two fives make a ten.

steps.narration: Now a 10, a 5 and a 1 together.
steps.feedback: 16. Add the big ones first. It is easier.

steps.narration: You have 20. The mango costs 15.
steps.feedback: 20 is more than 15, so you can buy it.
steps.prompt: Do you have enough to buy the mango?

steps.narration: The seller gives back what is left over. That is your change.
steps.feedback: 5 back. Now you know how to check your change.

steps.narration: Sometimes different coins make the same amount.
steps.feedback: 10 + 1 makes 11. 5 + 5 only makes 10.

recap.prompt: Two coins worth 5 each make…
What is one of those coins worth on its own?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Read the Bar Graph
content.objective: Read data from a simple bar graph.

questions.prompt: Which fruit got the most votes on the graph?
questions.correctFeedback: You read the graph. Apples have the tallest bar.
questions.retryFeedback: Find the tallest bar. Try again!

questions.prompt: What does the shortest bar tell you?
questions.correctFeedback: Shortest means fewest. Height is the whole message.
questions.retryFeedback: Taller means more, so shorter means...? Try again!

questions.prompt: Apples got 8 votes and pears got 5. How many more for apples?
questions.correctFeedback: 3 more. Comparing bars is subtraction.
questions.retryFeedback: Take 5 away from 8. Try again!

questions.prompt: Why do we draw a graph instead of writing a list?

options.label: You can see the answer at a glance

questions.correctFeedback: At a glance. That is the whole point of a picture of numbers.
questions.retryFeedback: Which is faster to understand? Try again!

content.subject: Math
content.title: Add Within 20
content.objective: Solve additions within twenty.
content.parentNote: 'Make ten first' is the strategy to praise. Counting on fingers still works and is not a failure.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: What is 8 + 7?
questions.retryFeedback: Make ten first: 8 + 2, then 5. Try again!

questions.prompt: What is 9 + 6?
questions.correctFeedback: 15. Same answer as 8 + 7 — there are many roads to a number.
questions.retryFeedback: 9 + 1 is 10, then 5 more. Try again!

questions.prompt: What is 13 - 5?
questions.correctFeedback: 8. Hop back five from thirteen.
questions.retryFeedback: Count back: 12, 11, 10... Try again!

questions.prompt: Which pair adds to 20?
questions.correctFeedback: 12 and 8. Two tens' worth exactly.
questions.retryFeedback: How far is 12 from 20? Try again!

content.subject: Math
content.title: What Time?
content.objective: Read an o'clock time from a clock face.
content.parentNote: The little hand is the one that matters, and it is the one children read last. Point at it first.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: The little hand is on 6, big hand on 12. What time is it?
questions.correctFeedback: 6 o'clock. You read both hands.
questions.retryFeedback: The little hand shows the hour. Try again!

questions.prompt: Which hand tells you the hour?
questions.correctFeedback: The little one, always. The big one counts minutes.
questions.retryFeedback: Which moves more slowly? Try again!

questions.prompt: Where does the big hand point at o'clock?
questions.correctFeedback: Straight up. That is what makes it 'o'clock'.
questions.retryFeedback: Picture 3 o'clock in your head. Try again!

questions.prompt: School starts at 8 o'clock. The little hand points at...
questions.correctFeedback: The 8. Hour on the little hand, every time.
questions.retryFeedback: Which hand names the hour? Try again!

content.subject: Math
content.title: Coins and Tens
content.objective: Count coins and read two-digit numbers.
content.parentNote: Real coins beat pictures here. Counting a handful in fives and tens is the same skill as place value.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: Two 5-coins. How much is that?
questions.correctFeedback: 10. Counting in fives: 5, 10.
questions.retryFeedback: 5, then 5 more. Try again!

questions.prompt: How many tens are in 47?
questions.correctFeedback: 4 tens and 7 ones. The first digit counts tens.
questions.retryFeedback: Look at the first digit. Try again!

questions.prompt: Which is more: 38 or 83?
questions.correctFeedback: 83. Same digits, but 8 tens beats 3 tens.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare the tens before the ones. Try again!

questions.prompt: You have 10 and spend 4. How much is left?
questions.correctFeedback: 6. Money problems are just subtraction wearing a hat.
questions.retryFeedback: Count back 4 from 10. Try again!

content.subject: Math
content.title: The Coin Jar
content.objective: Count money along in a story.
content.parentNote: Count along out loud in fives. Saying the numbers is what makes them stick.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Lila is saving coins in a jar. She wants a kite.
On Monday she puts in a 5-coin. That is 5.
On Tuesday another 5-coin. Count with her: 5, 10!
The kite costs 10. She has exactly enough.

pages.narration: Lila is saving coins in a jar. She wants a kite.
On Monday she puts in a 5-coin. That is 5.
On Tuesday another 5-coin. Count with her: 5, 10!
The kite costs 10. She has exactly enough.
But at the shop she sees a smaller kite for 5.
She buys the one she saved for, and keeps counting. Off it flies!

content.subject: Math
content.title: Ten O'Clock Exactly
content.objective: Read o'clock times through a story.
content.parentNote: Point at a real clock while you read. The little hand is the one to name first.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

Eight o'clock. Two whole hours to wait. He sighs.
He helps in the garden until the big hand comes round again.
Ten o'clock, and there is his friend at the gate. Right on time!

pages.narration: Kofi is meeting his friend at the park at 10 o'clock.
He checks the clock. The little hand is on 8.
Eight o'clock. Two whole hours to wait. He sighs.
He helps in the garden until the big hand comes round again.

Ten o'clock, and there is his friend at the gate. Right on time!

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Silent-e and Vowel Teams
content.objective: Read words with silent-e and vowel teams.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Read this word slowly: cap. /c/ /a/ /p/.
steps.feedback: Short and quick. The a says /a/.

steps.narration: Now watch. We add one letter at the end: cape.
steps.feedback: The word changed, and so did the middle sound.

steps.narration: Read it again: cape. The new e is silent. You never say it out loud.
steps.feedback: cape. The e is there but stays quiet.

steps.narration: Here is the magic: silent e makes the vowel read its own name. A says 'ay'.
steps.feedback: cap becomes cape. hop becomes hope.

steps.narration: Look for the quiet e at the end of the word.
steps.feedback: hope has it. hop and hopping do not.
steps.prompt: Which word has a silent e?

steps.narration: There is a second way vowels help each other. Two vowels together, one sound: rain.
steps.feedback: That is called a vowel team.

steps.narration: Find the two letters doing the work in rain.
steps.feedback: a and i together say /ay/.

steps.narration: Listen for that same /ay/ sound in another word.
steps.feedback: train! Same team, same sound.
steps.prompt: Which word has the same sound as rain?

steps.narration: Once you spot a team you can read a whole family: rain, pain, mail, tail.
steps.feedback: Four new words from one pattern.

steps.narration: Read this sentence: 'The tail is long.'
steps.feedback: tail. A and i again. You are reading with patterns now.
steps.prompt: Which word has a vowel team?

recap.prompt: Add silent-e to cap. What word do you get?
Which sound do the letters a and i make in rain?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Short and Long Vowels
content.objective: Hear short and long vowel sounds.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'cap' has a short a. Tap 'cap'.
steps.feedback: '/a/. Short a, cap!'

steps.narration: 'cape' has a long a. Tap 'cape'.
steps.feedback: '/ay/. Long a, cape! The e makes a say its name.'

steps.narration: 'kit' has a short i. Tap 'kit'.
steps.feedback: /i/. Short i, kit!

steps.narration: Watch: add a silent e and the vowel says its own name.
steps.feedback: kit becomes kite. One letter, whole new word.

steps.narration: Tap 'kite'. Listen for the long i.
steps.feedback: /eye/. Long i. The e did that!

steps.narration: One of these has a long vowel: hat, hate, ham. Tap it.
steps.feedback: hate. The silent e gives it away.

steps.narration: Does 'cap' or 'cape' have the long a? Tap 'cape'.
steps.feedback: cape. Same three letters plus an e.

steps.narration: Short vowels say their sound; long vowels say their name.
steps.feedback: A silent e at the end is your clue.

recap.prompt: Which word has the short a sound?
What does silent-e do to the vowel?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Consonant Blends
content.objective: Read words that start with blends.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Sometimes two letters stand side by side and you hear both. Listen: bl in black.
steps.feedback: /b/ and /l/, close together but both there.

steps.narration: Say black slowly and listen to the very start.
steps.feedback: bl. That is a blend.

steps.narration: A blend is two sounds, not one new sound.
steps.feedback: 2 sounds. You can hear them both if you go slowly.
steps.prompt: How many sounds do you hear in 'bl'?

steps.narration: Blends come in families too: st in stop, star, stand.
steps.feedback: Learn one blend, unlock many words.

steps.narration: Which of these begins with that st sound?
steps.feedback: star. sun starts with just /s/.

steps.narration: Blends can hide at the end of a word too. Listen to the end of hand: /n/ /d/.
steps.feedback: nd. Both sounds, right at the finish.

steps.narration: Say each one and listen to the last part.
steps.feedback: sand ends with nd.

steps.narration: Here is a new word to sound out: frog.
steps.feedback: fr at the front. /f/ then /r/.
steps.prompt: Which blend do you see in 'frog'?

steps.narration: bl, st, nd, fr. You can now sound out words you have never seen before.
steps.feedback: That is what blends are for.

recap.prompt: How many sounds does the blend bl make?
Which blend begins the word star: st or bl?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Read for Meaning
content.objective: Answer who and what about a sentence.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Read: 'The girl kicks the ball.' Who kicks? Tap the girl.
steps.feedback: The girl kicks it.

steps.narration: What does she kick? Tap the ball.
steps.feedback: The ball! You understood it.

steps.narration: Read: 'The boy feeds the cat.' Who feeds? Tap the boy.
steps.feedback: The boy. You found the who.

steps.narration: Watch: every sentence answers who, and what they did.
steps.feedback: Find those two and you have understood it.

steps.narration: In 'The girl reads a book', tap what she reads.
steps.feedback: The book. That is the what.

steps.narration: 'The dog runs to the river.' Tap where it runs to.
steps.feedback: The river. Sentences can answer where, too.

steps.narration: In 'The cat sleeps on the bed', who sleeps? Tap the cat.
steps.feedback: The cat. You asked the question yourself.

steps.narration: Who, what, where — three questions for any sentence.

content.subject: Science

steps.narration: A butterfly does not start as a butterfly. It starts as a tiny egg on a leaf.

steps.narration: Then the butterfly lays eggs, and it all begins again.

content.subject: Writing & Grammar
content.title: Nouns, Verbs, Adjectives
content.objective: Tell the difference between word types.

steps.narration: A noun is a person, place, or thing. Tap the noun: 'The happy dog runs.'
steps.feedback: 'dog' is the noun!

steps.narration: A verb is an action. Tap it.
steps.feedback: 'runs' is the verb!

steps.narration: An adjective describes. Tap it.
steps.feedback: 'happy' is the adjective!

steps.narration: In 'The small bird sings', tap the noun.
steps.feedback: 'bird' — a thing. That is the noun.

steps.narration: Watch: the noun is who or what, the verb is what it does, the adjective describes.
steps.feedback: Three jobs. Every sentence uses at least two.

steps.narration: In the same sentence, tap the word that describes the bird.
steps.feedback: 'small'. Adjectives tell you which one or what kind.

steps.narration: Now the action. Tap what the bird does.
steps.feedback: 'sings'. That is the verb.

steps.narration: In 'A red car stops', which word is the noun? Tap 'car'.
steps.feedback: 'car'. You sorted three word types by yourself.

steps.narration: Noun names, verb acts, adjective describes.

content.subject: Writing & Grammar
content.title: Nouns: Naming Words
content.objective: Identify nouns (people, places, things).
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A noun names a person, place, or thing. Tap the noun: 'dog'.
steps.feedback: 'dog' is a thing. A noun!

steps.narration: Tap the noun in 'I go to school'. (school)
steps.feedback: 'school' is a place. A noun!

steps.narration: A noun can be a person. Tap the noun in 'The teacher smiles'.
steps.feedback: 'teacher' — a person. Still a noun.

steps.narration: Watch: person, place or thing. If you can put 'the' in front, it is usually a noun.
steps.feedback: A handy test you can run in your head.

steps.narration: Tap the noun in 'We walk to the river'.
steps.feedback: 'river' — a place. Nouns can be places.

steps.narration: Two nouns hide in 'The girl holds a book'. Tap the second one.
steps.feedback: 'book'. A sentence can hold more than one.

steps.narration: Which is a noun: 'jump' or 'chair'? Tap 'chair'.
steps.feedback: 'chair' — a thing. 'jump' is an action.

steps.narration: Person, place or thing — that is a noun.

content.subject: Writing & Grammar
content.title: Verbs: Action Words
content.objective: Identify verbs (action words).
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Some words are things. Some words are doings. A doing word is a verb.
steps.feedback: run, jump, eat. All verbs.

steps.narration: One of these you can do. The other you sit on.
steps.feedback: jump is the action. A chair is a thing.

steps.narration: Every sentence needs a verb, or nothing happens in it.
steps.feedback: 'The girl runs.' Without runs, the girl just stands there.

steps.narration: Find the doing word in this sentence: 'The dog barks.'
steps.feedback: barks. That is what the dog does.

steps.narration: Verbs are not always loud or fast. Quiet things are verbs too: think, sleep, wait.
steps.feedback: If it is something you do, it is a verb.

steps.narration: You lie still when you do this one, but you are still doing it.
steps.feedback: Sleep is a verb.

steps.narration: Try a longer sentence: 'Amina reads a book.'
steps.feedback: reads. Amina is the person, book is the thing, reads is the doing.

steps.narration: Change the verb and you change what happens. 'The bird sings.' 'The bird flies.'
steps.feedback: Same bird, two different actions.

steps.narration: Only one of these can finish the sentence 'The bird ___.'
steps.feedback: flies. Blue and table are not doings.

content.subject: Writing & Grammar

steps.feedback: 'The big red' has no verb, so it says nothing yet.

steps.narration: Add a describing word: 'The' + 'small' + 'cat' + 'sleeps'.
steps.feedback: 'The small cat sleeps.' An adjective made it clearer.

steps.narration: One of these is not finished. Tap 'The tall green'.
steps.feedback: No verb, no sentence. You caught it.

steps.narration: Does every sentence need a capital at the start? Tap yes.
steps.feedback: Yes. Capital to open, period to close.

steps.narration: A noun, a verb, a capital and a period.

content.subject: Creativity & Tech
content.title: Code a Jump (Scratch Jr. style)

steps.narration: Drag move right, then jump. Press the green flag.
steps.feedback: The cat moves and jumps. You animated it.

steps.narration: Add a sound block at the end and run again.
steps.feedback: Meow. Your sequence plays in order.

steps.feedback: It will not guess what you meant. That is a feature, not a fault.

content.subject: Creativity & Tech
content.title: Loops Save Steps
content.objective: Use a loop to repeat code.

steps.feedback: Four sides. A square from a loop.

steps.narration: Loops save us from writing the same step over and over.
steps.feedback: Smart coding!

steps.narration: A loop is a promise: do this exact thing, this exact number of times.
steps.feedback: Four lines become one, and changing four becomes changing one.

steps.narration: To draw a triangle you repeat 'forward, turn'. How many times?
steps.feedback: 3. One repeat for each side.

steps.narration: And for a hexagon, which has six sides?
steps.feedback: 6. The shape decides the number, every time.

steps.narration: Someone looped 'forward, turn' 4 times and got a line, not a square. Tap the problem.
steps.feedback: The turn was zero degrees. A loop repeats a mistake perfectly too.

steps.narration: Rewrite this with a loop: forward, forward, forward, forward.
steps.feedback: Repeat forward x4. One block instead of four.

steps.narration: Find a loop in your own day: something you repeat a set number of times.
steps.feedback: Brushing every tooth, climbing every stair. Loops are everywhere.

recap.prompt: How many times do you repeat 'forward, turn' for a square?

content.subject: Creativity & Tech
content.title: If-Then Choices

steps.narration: An if-then rule only runs when its question is true. Otherwise it is skipped.
steps.feedback: The computer checks first and acts second. Always in that order.

steps.narration: Build the rule: if the cup is empty, then fill it.
steps.feedback: Condition first, action second. That is the whole shape.

steps.narration: The cup is full. Tap what the rule does now.
steps.feedback: Nothing at all. A false condition means the action never runs.

steps.narration: The light is not red. Tap what an 'else' branch is for.
steps.feedback: What to do when the answer is no. Without it, nothing happens.

steps.narration: Build one with both branches: if it is dark, turn on the light; else, turn it off.
steps.feedback: Now every case is covered. That is what makes a rule complete.

steps.narration: Say a house rule out loud as if-then. 'If it is raining, then take a coat.'
steps.feedback: Most rules people live by are already written this way.

pages.narration: Dayo's robot was supposed to draw a square. It drew a straight line.
'It's broken,' said Dayo. He tried a different robot. Same line.
So he ran his code one block at a time and watched.
Forward worked. Turn worked — but the turn was set to zero degrees.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Multiplication as Arrays
content.objective: Understand multiplication as equal groups / arrays.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Make 3 rows of 4 dots. Tap to add a row.
steps.feedback: Array fills in row by row.

steps.narration: Three rows of four. How many altogether?
steps.feedback: 12. Three equal rows of four, so 3 × 4 = 12.

steps.narration: Try it your way: build 2 × 5.
steps.feedback: Nice. 2 rows of 5 makes 10.

steps.narration: An array is just equal rows. Every row has to hold the same amount.
steps.feedback: Equal rows are what makes it multiplication and not just adding.

steps.narration: Build 4 rows of 3. How many dots altogether?
steps.feedback: 12. Four rows of three is 4 × 3 = 12.

steps.narration: Now turn it: 3 rows of 4. How many now?
steps.feedback: 12 again. Turning an array does not change how many.

steps.narration: Someone built 3 rows of 4 but put 5 in the last row. Tap the row that is wrong.
steps.feedback: Unequal rows are not an array. That is the whole rule.

steps.narration: Windows, egg boxes, tiled floors — arrays are everywhere once you look.
steps.feedback: Find one today and say its multiplication out loud.

recap.prompt: 3 rows of 4 dots make how many altogether?
2 rows of 5 make how many?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Add Two-Digit Numbers
content.objective: Add with regrouping.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 24 + 18. Add ones: 4 + 8 = 12. Carry the ten!
steps.feedback: 'Write 2, carry 1 ten.'

steps.narration: Add tens: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. So 42.
Regrouping has one rule: ten ones become one ten, and the ten moves left.
steps.feedback: That is the only new idea. Everything else is adding you already know.

steps.narration: Try one: 37 + 25. Start with the ones. 7 + 5 = ?
steps.feedback: 12. So write 2 and carry one ten.

steps.narration: Now the tens, and do not forget the one you carried. 3 + 2 + 1 = ?
Someone wrote 37 + 25 = 512. Tap what they forgot to do.
steps.feedback: They wrote both answers side by side instead of carrying. Very common.

steps.narration: Your turn, no help: 46 + 28.
steps.feedback: 74. Ones made 14, so you carried a ten.

steps.narration: Add up two prices in a shop today, in your head.
steps.feedback: Carrying is the part that makes it fast.

recap.prompt: When the ones add up past ten, what do you do?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Subtract Two-Digit Numbers
content.objective: Subtract with regrouping.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 52 - 27. Ones: 2 is less than 7, so borrow a ten.
Borrowing is regrouping backwards: one ten becomes ten ones.
steps.feedback: You are not taking anything away. You are only changing its shape.

steps.narration: Try one: 63 - 28. The ones: 3 is smaller than 8, so borrow. 13 - 8 = ?
steps.feedback: 5. You borrowed a ten to make 13.

steps.narration: The 6 tens is now 5, because you lent one. 5 - 2 = ?
Someone did 63 - 28 and got 45. Tap the column they got wrong.
steps.feedback: They borrowed but forgot to take the ten away from the 6.

steps.narration: Your turn: 52 - 17.
steps.feedback: 35. Borrow once, then subtract both columns.

steps.narration: Work out the change from a note today before the shopkeeper does.
steps.feedback: Subtraction with borrowing is most of what money asks of you.

recap.prompt: When the top digit is too small, what do you do?

steps.narration: A compound word keeps both meanings inside it. Look for them.
steps.feedback: A 'sunflower' is a flower that follows the sun. The word tells you.

steps.feedback: Football. A ball you play with your foot.

steps.feedback: Bed and room. The room where the bed is.

steps.narration: One of these is not a compound word. Tap it: butterfly, carpet, rainbow.

steps.narration: Tap the compound word in this sentence: 'The postman crossed the playground.'

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Prefixes un- and re-
content.objective: Use prefixes to change meaning.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'un' means 'not'. 'unhappy' means not happy. Tap 'unhappy'.
steps.feedback: 'un-happy', not happy.

steps.narration: 're' means 'again'. 'redo' means do again.
steps.feedback: 're-do'. Do it again.

steps.narration: A prefix goes on the front and changes the meaning without changing the word.
steps.feedback: The root word stays whole underneath. That is how you can still read it.

steps.narration: Make a word that means 'not kind'. Drag a prefix onto 'kind'.
steps.feedback: Unkind. 'un' turns a word into its opposite.

steps.narration: Now make one that means 'read again'.
steps.feedback: Reread. 're' means again, every time.

steps.narration: 'Unlock' really does mean not locked. But someone said 'uncle' means 'not cle'. Tap why that is wrong.
steps.feedback: 'cle' is not a word. A prefix only counts if a real word is left behind.

steps.narration: Tap the word that means 'did not do it right the first time'.
steps.feedback: Redo. You only redo something you did once already.

steps.narration: Two prefixes, and you can now read hundreds of words you have never met.
steps.feedback: That is what prefixes are for.

recap.prompt: What does the prefix un- mean?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Context Clues
content.objective: Use the sentence to guess a word.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'The thirsty dog drank from its bowl.' What does 'thirsty' mean?
steps.feedback: Needing a drink. The sentence gave you the clue.

steps.narration: Other words give us clues.
steps.feedback: Smart reading!

steps.narration: When a word is new, the sentence around it is the clue.
steps.feedback: Good readers guess from context first and check the dictionary second.

steps.narration: 'The bridge was so narrow only one person could pass.' Tap what narrow means.
steps.feedback: Not wide. The rest of the sentence told you, not the word itself.

steps.narration: 'She was famished, so she ate two whole bowls.' Tap what famished means.
steps.feedback: Very hungry. What she did next gave it away.

steps.narration: 'The dog was enormous.' Tap the word in this sentence that is NOT a clue.
steps.feedback: 'The'. One short sentence often has no clue at all — read the next one.

steps.narration: 'It was drizzling, so we did not need umbrellas.' Tap what drizzling means.
steps.feedback: Raining only a little. 'So we did not need' is the clue.

steps.narration: Next time you hit a word you do not know, finish the sentence first.
steps.feedback: Most of the time the sentence has already told you.

content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'Maya played at the beach.' Who is the character?
steps.feedback: Maya. The character is who the story is about.

steps.narration: Where is the setting? Tap the beach.
steps.feedback: The beach is the setting.

steps.narration: Character is who. Setting is where and when. Every story has both.
steps.feedback: Change the setting and the same character has a different story.

steps.narration: 'On a cold night, Ravi waited at the station.' Tap the character.
steps.feedback: Ravi. The person the story is following.

steps.narration: Same sentence. Tap the two words that give you the setting.
steps.feedback: 'Cold night' and 'station' — when, and where.

steps.narration: Someone said the setting of that story is 'waiting'. Tap why not.
steps.feedback: Waiting is what happens, not where. That is plot, not setting.

steps.narration: Sort these into character and setting: Amina, the market, midnight, the old dog.
steps.feedback: Amina and the dog are who. The market and midnight are where and when.

steps.narration: At the end of your next story, name the character and setting out loud.
steps.feedback: Two questions that work on every book ever written.

recap.prompt: 'Maya played at the beach.' Who is the character?
In that sentence, where is the setting?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Fact or Opinion
content.objective: Tell a fact from an opinion.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'The sky is blue' is a fact. We can check it. Tap 'fact'.
steps.feedback: A fact can be proven.

steps.narration: 'Blue is the best color' is an opinion. What someone feels.
steps.feedback: An opinion is a feeling.

steps.narration: A fact can be checked, like the number of chairs in a room. An opinion cannot.
steps.feedback: That is the whole test: could someone go and find out?

steps.narration: 'This tree is ten metres tall.' Fact or opinion? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Fact. Somebody could count them.

steps.narration: 'This tree is ugly.' Fact or opinion? Tap your answer.
steps.feedback: Opinion. There is no way to measure ugly.

steps.narration: 'Everyone knows this soup is disgusting.' Tap the part that makes it an opinion.
steps.feedback: 'Disgusting'. Starting with 'everyone knows' does not turn a taste into a fact.

steps.narration: Tap the sentence that is a fact: 'Rain is wet' or 'Rainy days are sad'.
steps.feedback: Rain is wet. The other one is how someone feels about rain.

steps.narration: Listen for one opinion said like a fact on the radio today.
steps.feedback: Spotting the difference is most of thinking clearly.

recap.prompt: 'The sky is blue' can be checked, so it is a…
'Blue is the best colour' is what someone feels, so it is an…

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Main Idea and Details
content.objective: Find the main idea and supporting details.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A paragraph about bees tells what they eat and how they help flowers. The main idea is bees. Tap it.
steps.feedback: Bees. That is the main idea.

steps.narration: The details tell more about the main idea.
steps.feedback: Main idea plus details. Great!

steps.narration: The main idea is what the whole paragraph is about. Details prove it.
steps.feedback: If you removed a detail the paragraph survives. Remove the main idea and it collapses.

steps.narration: A paragraph says bees make honey, pollinate flowers and live in hives. Tap the main idea.
steps.feedback: What bees do. Each sentence is one example of it.

steps.narration: Same paragraph. Tap one supporting detail.
steps.feedback: Any of the three. Details are the evidence, not the point.

steps.narration: Someone said the main idea is 'honey'. Tap why that is too small.
steps.feedback: Honey is one detail. A main idea has to cover all of them.

steps.narration: Drag these under the right heading: 'Volcanoes are dangerous' / 'lava burns' / 'ash blocks the sun'.
steps.feedback: The first is the main idea; the other two are why it is true.

steps.narration: Read one paragraph tonight and say its main idea in six words or fewer.
steps.feedback: If you cannot, you have not found it yet.

recap.prompt: A paragraph tells what an insect eats and how it helps plants. The main idea is…
What do details do?

questions.prompt: Which word is a compound word?

pages.narration: Sam trained all week for the big race. He was nervous but ready.
At the start, he tripped! But he got up and kept running.
His knee stung and the others were far ahead.
He thought about stopping. Then he thought about the week of training.
He ran the last stretch slower than he had ever run it, and did not stop.
He didn't win, but he finished, and felt proud. Trying hard matters most!

pages.narration: Lena hit a word she had never seen: 'The old bridge was precarious.'
She almost stopped to ask. Instead she read the next sentence.
'Nobody crossed it after dark, and two planks were missing.'
Missing planks. Nobody crossing. Precarious must mean unsafe.

She had been right. The sentence had told her all along.

content.subject: Science
content.title: Food Chains
content.objective: Build a simple food chain.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Start the chain: the sun gives energy to the ___?
steps.feedback: Grass. The sun feeds the grass.

steps.narration: Grass → rabbit → ___?
steps.feedback: Fox. Energy passes along the food chain.

steps.narration: Every food chain starts at the sun. Nothing else makes its own energy.
steps.feedback: Plants catch it; everything else has to eat to get some.

steps.narration: Build the chain: sun, grass, rabbit, fox. Drag them into order.
steps.feedback: Each arrow means 'is eaten by'. Energy only travels one way.

steps.narration: Someone put the fox before the rabbit. Tap what goes wrong.
steps.feedback: The fox does not feed the rabbit. The arrows would point backwards.

steps.narration: If every rabbit disappeared, tap what happens to the foxes.
steps.feedback: They go hungry. Remove one link and everything above it suffers.

steps.narration: Build a sea chain: sun, seaweed, small fish, seal.
steps.feedback: Same shape, different animals. Every chain works this way.

steps.narration: Trace your own dinner back to the sun tonight.
steps.feedback: It takes fewer steps than you would think.

recap.prompt: Where does a food chain get its energy first?
Grass, then rabbit, then…

content.subject: Science
content.title: Habitats
content.objective: Match animals to their habitats.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A fish lives in water. Drag the fish to the pond.
steps.feedback: 'Water is its habitat.'

steps.narration: A camel lives in the desert. Drag it there.
steps.feedback: 'A habitat gives animals what they need.'

steps.narration: A habitat is not just a place. It is food, water, shelter and the right weather.
steps.feedback: Take away any one of the four and the animal cannot stay.

steps.narration: Drag the polar bear to where its thick fur is useful.
steps.feedback: The ice. Its body is built for the cold, not just used to it.

steps.narration: Now the camel. Drag it to the habitat that suits it.
steps.feedback: The desert. It stores water and its feet spread on sand.

steps.narration: Tap what would happen if you moved the polar bear to the desert.
steps.feedback: It would overheat. The fur that saves it in one place kills it in another.

steps.narration: Tap the one thing a habitat does not have to provide: food, shelter, friends, water.
steps.feedback: Friends. Many animals live alone their whole lives.

steps.narration: Name the habitat just outside your door, and one animal that fits it.
steps.feedback: A garden, a street, a rooftop — all of them are habitats.

recap.prompt: Where is a fish's habitat?
What does a habitat give an animal?

content.subject: Science
content.title: Food Chains
content.objective: Follow energy through a food chain.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: The sun feeds the grass. Tap the grass.
steps.feedback: Plants make food from sunlight.

steps.narration: A rabbit eats grass; a fox eats the rabbit. Tap to follow the chain.
steps.feedback: 'Sun → grass → rabbit → fox. A food chain.'

steps.narration: Energy gets smaller at every step. Most of it is lost as heat and movement.
steps.feedback: That is why chains are short, and why there are always fewer foxes than rabbits.

steps.narration: Tap which there are more of in a field: grass plants or rabbits.
steps.feedback: Grass, by far. Each level needs a much bigger level under it.

steps.narration: Tap the animal that would need the biggest area to survive: rabbit or fox.
steps.feedback: The fox. It has to find enough rabbits, and rabbits are spread out.

steps.narration: Stack the field into a pyramid: grass at the bottom, then rabbits, then foxes.
steps.feedback: A pyramid, never a tower. Each layer is smaller than the one below.

steps.narration: Tap what happens to the grass if all the rabbits leave.
steps.feedback: It grows thick and wild. Chains work downwards as well as up.

steps.narration: Look for a food chain on your street: a plant, an insect, a bird.
steps.feedback: Three links is a real chain. You do not need a jungle.

recap.prompt: What do plants make their food from?
Sun, grass, rabbit, fox is an example of a…

content.subject: Science
content.title: States of Matter
content.objective: Compare solids, liquids, and gases.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A rock is solid. It keeps its shape. Tap the solid.
steps.feedback: 'Solid. Firm.'

steps.narration: Juice is liquid; air is gas. Tap each.
steps.feedback: 'Liquid flows; gas spreads out.'

steps.narration: A rock, water, air: solid, liquid and gas differ by how tightly the tiny bits hold together.
steps.feedback: Same water, three states. Heat loosens it; cold tightens it up again.

steps.narration: Sort these: a stone, milk, steam, a spoon, air.
steps.feedback: Two solids, one liquid, two gases. Shape is the giveaway.

steps.narration: Tap the state that takes the shape of any container you pour it into.
steps.feedback: Liquid. A solid keeps its own shape; a gas fills the whole space.

steps.narration: Someone said ice and water are different substances. Tap why that is wrong.
steps.feedback: Same substance, different state. Melting changes the state, not the stuff.

steps.narration: Tap what you would add to turn ice into steam.
steps.feedback: Heat, twice. Solid to liquid, then liquid to gas.

steps.narration: Watch a kettle or a cold glass today and name the state change out loud.
steps.feedback: Both are the water cycle happening in your kitchen.

recap.prompt: A rock keeps its shape, so it is a…
Juice flows and fills its cup, so it is a…

content.subject: Science
content.title: The Water Cycle
content.objective: Learn how water moves in a cycle.
content.parentNote: Watch a puddle shrink on a sunny day — that's evaporation.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: The sun heats water. It evaporates into the air. Tap to evaporate.
steps.feedback: Up it goes as vapor.

steps.narration: It cools into clouds (Condense), then falls as rain (Precipitate).
steps.feedback: 'Evaporate, condense, precipitate. The water cycle.'

steps.narration: The water cycle has no start and no end. That is what makes it a cycle.
steps.feedback: The water in your glass has been round it more times than anyone can count.

steps.narration: Put the four stages in order: condense, evaporate, collect, precipitate.
steps.feedback: Evaporate, condense, precipitate, collect — then round again.

steps.narration: Tap what lifts the water and drives the whole cycle.
steps.feedback: The sun. Without it water would never rise at all.

steps.narration: Tap what a cloud actually is.
steps.feedback: Water that has cooled back into tiny drops. Not steam, and not smoke.

steps.narration: Someone said rain is new water. Tap why that cannot be true.
steps.feedback: It is the same water going round. Nothing new is made, only moved.

steps.narration: Find the cycle in one day: a puddle gone by noon, a cold window at night.
steps.feedback: Evaporation and condensation, ten metres from where you sleep.

recap.prompt: The sun heats water and it rises into the air. That is…
Water vapour cools into clouds. That is…

content.subject: Science
content.title: Magnets
content.objective: Explore what magnets do.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Magnets pull some metals. Tap to pull the paperclip.
steps.feedback: Click. The magnet pulls it.

steps.narration: Two same poles push apart. Tap to feel the push.
steps.feedback: Magnets push and pull.

steps.narration: Magnets pull iron and steel — not every metal, and no plastic or wood at all.
steps.feedback: Aluminium is a metal and a magnet ignores it completely.

steps.narration: Tap the one a magnet will pick up: a paperclip, a coin, a rubber band.
steps.feedback: The paperclip. It is steel, and steel has iron in it.

steps.narration: Two north poles are brought together. Tap what they do.
steps.feedback: Push apart. Same poles repel; opposite poles attract.

steps.narration: Tap whether a magnet still works through a sheet of paper.
steps.feedback: It does. Magnetism passes through things that are not magnetic.

steps.narration: Someone said magnets attract all metals. Tap the metal that proves them wrong.
steps.feedback: Aluminium, or copper. Most metals are not magnetic at all.

steps.narration: Test five things at home with a fridge magnet and predict each one first.
steps.feedback: Predicting before testing is the whole of science.

recap.prompt: What do magnets do to some metals?
What do two of the same poles do?

pages.narration: After the rain there was a puddle the size of a door.
By noon it had shrunk to the size of a plate.
Nothing drank it. The sun had lifted it into the air, one drop at a time.
High up it cooled and gathered with other water into a cloud.
That night the cloud grew heavy and it rained again.
In the morning the puddle was back. The same water, going round.

steps.narration: Capitals mark names: people, places, days, months. Not ordinary things.

steps.narration: If-else covers both answers. A lone 'if' leaves the closed door doing nothing.
steps.feedback: That is the whole difference, and it is where most bugs live.

steps.narration: Build it: if the cup is empty, fill it; else, leave it.
steps.feedback: Condition, then action, then the other action. Every case covered.

steps.narration: The gate is already open. Tap which branch of 'if open, go through; else knock' runs.
steps.feedback: The first. The else branch is skipped entirely, not run quietly.

steps.narration: Someone wrote 'if it is cold, wear a coat' with no else. Tap what is missing.
steps.feedback: Nothing happens when it is warm — which may be fine, or may be the bug.

steps.narration: Write an if-else for a traffic light: red, and everything else.
steps.feedback: If red, stop; else, go carefully. Two branches, no gaps.

steps.narration: Say one of your own rules as if-else, including what happens when it is false.
steps.feedback: Most people only ever say the 'if' half out loud.

recap.prompt: If the gate is open you go through. Else you…
What does if-else let a program do?

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: Variables
content.objective: Store a value in a variable.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A variable is a box that holds a value. Put 5 into 'score'. Tap to set it.
steps.feedback: score = 5.

steps.narration: Change it: score + 3. Now score holds 8.
steps.feedback: Variables can change.

steps.narration: A variable is a labelled box. The label stays; what is inside can change.
steps.feedback: That is why a program can count without knowing the number in advance.

steps.narration: 'score' holds 5. The program does score + 3. What does score hold now?
steps.feedback: 8. The box was emptied and refilled with the new total.

steps.narration: Then the program does score + score. What does it hold now?
steps.feedback: 16. It read its own value twice, then stored the answer.

steps.narration: Someone set score to 5, then to 9, and expected 14. Tap their mistake.
steps.feedback: Setting replaces; it does not add. The 5 was gone the moment 9 arrived.

steps.narration: Build a counter: set 'lives' to 3, then take one away when the player is hit.
steps.feedback: Now the game can tell how many are left without you writing it down.

steps.narration: Name three variables in a game you play: score, lives, level.
steps.feedback: Every number on the screen that changes is one of these.

recap.prompt: What does a variable do?
score is 5, then you add 3. What does it hold now?

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: Functions
content.objective: Group steps into a reusable function.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A function names a group of steps so you can reuse them. Make 'wave' = raise arm, lower arm. Tap to call 'wave'.
steps.feedback: The robot waves.

steps.narration: Call 'wave' again. No need to rewrite the steps!
steps.feedback: Functions save work.

steps.narration: A function is a name for a group of steps, so you write them once.
steps.feedback: Fix the function and every place that calls it is fixed too.

steps.narration: Make a function called 'jump': crouch, spring, land.
steps.feedback: Three steps, one name. Now 'jump' means all three.

steps.narration: You call 'jump' four times. How many steps does the robot actually do?
steps.feedback: 12. Three steps inside, called four times.

steps.narration: The jump is too small everywhere in the game. Tap the one place to fix it.
steps.feedback: Inside the function. That is what functions are for.

steps.narration: Write a function 'greet' and call it twice from your program.
steps.feedback: Two calls, one definition. The program got shorter and clearer at once.

steps.narration: Name a routine in your morning that is really a function: 'get ready'.
steps.feedback: Two words that stand for eight steps everybody already knows.

recap.prompt: What does a function do?
Why is a function useful?

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: True or False
content.objective: Use boolean logic.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: '5 is greater than 3'. Is that true or false?
steps.feedback: True. 5 is more than 3.

steps.narration: 'A cat has wings' is false. Computers use true/false to decide.
steps.feedback: Boolean logic.

steps.narration: Every condition a computer checks comes back as just true or false.
steps.feedback: There is no 'maybe'. That is why a program can always decide.

steps.narration: Tap whether this is true or false: a spider has eight legs.
steps.feedback: True, and checkable. That is what makes it a condition and not an opinion.

steps.narration: Tap true or false: 7 is greater than 10.
steps.feedback: False. The computer does not argue, it just takes the else branch.

steps.narration: 'The sky is beautiful.' Tap why a computer cannot check this.
steps.feedback: Beautiful cannot be measured. Conditions need facts, not feelings.

steps.narration: Tap the one a program could actually test: 'the door is locked' or 'the room is cosy'.
steps.feedback: The lock. It is either shut or it is not, with nothing in between.

steps.narration: Ask three questions at dinner that can only be answered true or false.
steps.feedback: It is harder than it sounds, and that is the lesson.

recap.prompt: '5 is greater than 3' is…
'A cat has wings' is…

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: Plan an Algorithm
content.objective: Break a task into clear steps.
content.parentNote: Plan a everyday task as numbered steps together.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: To make a sandwich, list the steps in order. Drag them into an algorithm.
steps.feedback: A clear plan. An algorithm.

steps.narration: Good algorithms have steps in the right order.
steps.feedback: You think like a coder.

steps.narration: An algorithm is a recipe for bread, precise enough that someone else could follow it.
steps.feedback: If a step needs guessing, it is not finished yet.

steps.narration: Put these in order: butter the bread, take out two slices, put them together.
steps.feedback: Take out, butter, put together. Order is most of an algorithm.

steps.narration: A recipe says 'add the right amount of salt'. Tap why that is a bad step.
steps.feedback: 'Right' is not a measurement. The follower has to guess, so it will vary.

steps.narration: Tap the step that is out of order: wake up, eat breakfast, get out of bed.
steps.feedback: Getting out of bed comes before breakfast, not after.

steps.narration: Write a four-step algorithm for brushing your teeth, precise enough to follow.
steps.feedback: Now hand it to someone and watch. Every gap will show itself.

steps.narration: Give a grown-up exact steps to draw a house, without showing them.
steps.feedback: Whatever they draw is exactly what you actually said.

recap.prompt: A task broken into clear steps in order is an…
What makes an algorithm good?

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: Find the Bug
content.objective: Debug a short sequence.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Fixing it once fixes every place that uses it

questions.prompt: The robot should go forward then turn, but it spins in place. What is missing?
questions.correctFeedback: You spotted the missing step. It needs a forward move.
questions.retryFeedback: What makes it move ahead? Try again!

questions.prompt: A loop draws a square. How many times must it repeat?
questions.correctFeedback: One repeat per side, and a square has four.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the sides of the shape first.

questions.prompt: A robot stops one square short of the flag. What is the likely bug?
questions.correctFeedback: Off-by-one. The robot did exactly what it was told.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the steps against the squares.

questions.prompt: Why write a function instead of repeating the same three steps?

options.label: Fixing it once fixes every place that uses it

questions.correctFeedback: One definition, many calls. That is the whole benefit.
questions.retryFeedback: Speed is the same either way.

content.objective: Track a variable's value.

questions.correctFeedback: 4 + 2 = 6. The variable updated.

Holding a number that never changes

questions.correctFeedback: Variables earn their name by varying.
questions.retryFeedback: A number that never changes needs no box.

questions.retryFeedback: Is it sunny? If not, the else branch runs. Try again!

questions.correctFeedback: The else branch is skipped entirely, not run quietly.
questions.retryFeedback: Only one branch ever runs.

questions.retryFeedback: Count up from 7 and see whether you pass 10.

questions.prompt: Which could a program actually test?
questions.correctFeedback: Locked is either true or not. Cosy cannot be measured.
questions.retryFeedback: Conditions need facts, not feelings.

questions.correctFeedback: One per side, and a triangle has three.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the sides first.

questions.prompt: lives = 3, then lives = lives - 1, twice. What is lives?
questions.correctFeedback: Three, minus one, minus one again.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the step twice, not once.

questions.prompt: Is 'a spider has eight legs' true or false?
questions.correctFeedback: True, and checkable. That makes it a condition, not an opinion.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the legs on a picture of one.

questions.prompt: You call a three-step function four times. How many steps run?
questions.correctFeedback: Three inside, called four times.
questions.retryFeedback: Calling is not adding; it is repeating.

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: Robo's Recipe Function
content.objective: Why naming a group of steps changes everything.

Worse: when the recipe changed, Robo had to fix it in nine places.

Now a change goes in one place, and every batch gets it.
Robo adds a loop too: repeat 'bake' three times for three trays.
Now Robo just says 'bake'! Functions make code neat and reusable. Beep!

content.subject: Logic & Coding
content.title: The Sandwich Instructions
content.objective: An algorithm is only as good as its least precise step.
content.parentNote: Try it for real. Follow their instructions exactly, and no further.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Ife wrote instructions for making a sandwich and gave them to her uncle.
Step one said 'get the bread'. He picked up the whole loaf.
Step two said 'put on butter'. He put the butter on top of the loaf.
Ife laughed, then stopped. He had done exactly what she wrote.
She rewrote it: take two slices, spread butter on one side of each.
This time it worked. Precise is not fussy; it is the whole job.

pages.narration: Ife wrote instructions for making a sandwich and gave them to her uncle.
Step one said 'get the bread'. He picked up the whole loaf.
Step two said 'put on butter'. He put the butter on top of the loaf.
Ife laughed, then stopped. He had done exactly what she wrote.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Multiplication and Division Facts
content.objective: Connect multiplication and division.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 6 × 4 = ? Build the array and count.
steps.feedback: 24. Six groups of four.

steps.narration: So 24 ÷ 4 = ? Use the same fact backward.
steps.feedback: 6. Multiplication and division are linked.

steps.narration: Multiplication and division are the same fact read in two directions.
steps.feedback: 6 × 4 = 24 tells you 24 ÷ 4 = 6 without any new work.

steps.narration: You know 7 × 5 = 35. What is 35 divided by 5?
steps.feedback: 7. The same fact, turned around.

steps.narration: And what is 35 divided by 7?
steps.feedback: 5. Every multiplication gives you two divisions.

steps.narration: Someone said 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so 4 ÷ 24 = 6. Tap why that is wrong.
steps.feedback: Division does not flip like multiplication. The whole comes first.

steps.narration: Eight children share 32 mangoes equally. How many each?
steps.feedback: 4. Because 8 × 4 = 32, which you already knew.

steps.narration: Share something between everyone at home and say the division out loud.
steps.feedback: Sharing fairly is division, every single time.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Understanding Fractions
content.objective: See fractions as equal parts.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: A pizza cut in 4 equal parts: each is 1/4. Tap one quarter.
steps.feedback: 'One out of four. 1/4.'

steps.narration: The bottom number is the total parts; the top is how many we have.
steps.feedback: Fractions are equal parts.

steps.narration: The bottom number counts the parts the whole was cut into.
steps.feedback: The top number counts how many of those parts you are holding.

steps.narration: A cake is cut into 8 equal slices. How many slices is one whole cake?
steps.feedback: 8. Eight eighths make one whole, always.

steps.narration: Tap the pizza that is cut into quarters, not thirds.
steps.feedback: Four equal pieces. Count the cuts before you count the slices.

steps.narration: A cake was cut into 4 pieces, but one is much bigger. Tap why these are not quarters.
steps.feedback: Fractions need equal parts. Four pieces is not the same as four quarters.

steps.narration: You eat 3 slices of a cake cut into 8. Tap the fraction you ate.
steps.feedback: Three eighths. Top is what you took, bottom is what there was.

steps.narration: Cut a piece of fruit into equal parts and name each one out loud.
steps.feedback: Halves, thirds, quarters — you can see all three on one apple.

recap.prompt: A pizza cut into 4 equal parts: each piece is…
What does the bottom number of a fraction show?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Compare Fractions
content.objective: Compare fractions with the same whole.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Which is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4? Tap the bigger piece.
steps.feedback: '1/2 is bigger. Fewer pieces means bigger pieces.'

steps.narration: The more parts you cut, the smaller each part.
steps.feedback: Smart comparing!
steps.prompt: More parts means each part is…

steps.narration: With the same whole, more parts means each part is smaller.
steps.feedback: That is why 1/8 is less than 1/4, even though 8 is more than 4.

steps.narration: Tap the bigger piece: one third of a cake, or one sixth.
steps.feedback: A third. Cutting into six makes each piece half the size.

steps.narration: Tap which is more: 3/4 of a pizza or 2/4 of the same pizza.
steps.feedback: Three quarters. When the bottoms match, just compare the tops.

steps.narration: Someone said 1/5 is bigger than 1/3 because 5 is bigger. Tap the mistake.
steps.feedback: The bottom number counts cuts, not size. More cuts, smaller pieces.

steps.narration: Two children share one orange; three share another. Tap who gets more.
steps.feedback: The two. Half beats a third, every time.

steps.narration: Next time something is shared, work out the fraction before it is cut.
steps.feedback: Knowing your share in advance is the useful part.

recap.prompt: Which is bigger?
The more parts you cut, the smaller each part is. So more parts means…

content.subject: Math
content.title: Multiply by Tens
content.objective: Multiply by multiples of ten.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 3 × 10 = 30. Just add a zero! Tap 30.
3 × 20 is 3 × 2 = 6, then a zero: 60.
Multiplying by ten shifts every digit one place left. The zero fills the gap.
steps.feedback: It is not a trick. It is what place value means.

steps.narration: What is 7 × 10?
steps.feedback: 70. The 7 moved into the tens place.

steps.narration: What is 4 × 30?
steps.feedback: 120. Four threes is twelve, then the zero.

steps.narration: Someone worked out 6 × 20 as 62. Tap what they did wrong.
steps.feedback: They wrote the zero beside the 6 instead of multiplying by 2 first.

steps.narration: Five boxes hold 40 pencils each. How many pencils altogether?
steps.feedback: 200. Five fours is twenty, then the zero.

steps.narration: Work out the cost of ten of something in a shop, in your head.
steps.feedback: Tens are the one times table nobody needs to memorise.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Rounding
content.objective: Round to the nearest 10 and 100.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: Round 47 to the nearest ten. Is it closer to 40 or 50?
steps.feedback: 50. 47 is past halfway, so it rounds up.

steps.narration: Round 230 to the nearest 100: 200.
steps.feedback: Rounding makes numbers easier.

steps.narration: Rounding asks one question: which ten is this number nearer to?
steps.feedback: Exactly halfway is the only case that needs a rule, and the rule is: round up.

steps.narration: Round 47 to the nearest ten.
steps.feedback: 50. It is only 3 away from 50, but 7 away from 40.

steps.narration: Round 231 to the nearest hundred.
steps.feedback: 200. It has not reached the halfway mark of 250.

steps.narration: Someone rounded 45 down to 40 because 5 is small. Tap the rule they forgot.
steps.feedback: Exactly halfway rounds up. 45 becomes 50, not 40.

steps.narration: A shop has 178 apples. About how many is that, to the nearest hundred?
steps.feedback: 200. Rounding is for when close enough is genuinely enough.

steps.narration: Round the price of three things in a shop and add them in your head.
steps.feedback: You will be close enough to know if you can afford them.

recap.prompt: Round 47 to the nearest ten.
Round 230 to the nearest hundred.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Read a Bar Graph
content.objective: Read data from a bar graph.
content.parentNote: Make a simple bar graph of something at home together.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: The graph shows pets in the class. Which pet has the tallest bar?
steps.feedback: Dogs. The tallest bar means the most.

steps.narration: How many more dogs than cats? Compare the bars.
steps.feedback: You read the data.
steps.prompt: How do you find 'how many more'?

steps.narration: A bar graph turns counting into looking. The tallest bar is the biggest group.
steps.feedback: The scale up the side is what turns a picture back into a number.

steps.narration: The dog bar reaches 9 and the cat bar reaches 5. How many more dogs?
steps.feedback: 4. Comparing bars is subtraction you can see.

steps.narration: Dogs 9, cats 5, fish 2. How many pets in the class altogether?
steps.feedback: 16. Adding the bars gives the whole class.

steps.narration: Someone read a bar as 5 without checking the scale. Tap what could go wrong.
steps.feedback: If each step is worth 2, that bar is 10. The scale changes everything.

steps.narration: Tap the question a bar graph cannot answer: 'which pet is most common?' or 'which pet is nicest?'
steps.feedback: Nicest is an opinion. Graphs count things; they do not judge them.

steps.narration: Count something at home three ways and draw the bars: shoes, cups, books.
steps.feedback: A graph you drew from your own counting is easier to trust.

recap.prompt: On a bar graph, which bar shows the most?
How do you find 'how many more'?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Simile and Metaphor
content.objective: Spot figurative language.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

steps.narration: 'As brave as a lion' compares using the word 'as'. Which kind of comparison is it?
steps.feedback: A simile. It compares using 'like' or 'as'.

steps.narration: 'The classroom was a zoo' calls it something it is not. Which kind is it?
steps.feedback: A metaphor. It says one thing is another.

steps.narration: A simile says a voice is *like* thunder. A metaphor says the classroom *is* a zoo.
steps.feedback: Both are ways of explaining by borrowing something you already know.

steps.narration: 'Her voice was like thunder.' Tap which kind of comparison this is.
steps.feedback: A simile — the word 'like' gives it away every time.

steps.narration: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Tap which kind this is.
steps.feedback: A metaphor. It does not say like a zoo; it says it was one.

steps.narration: Someone read 'the classroom was a zoo' and asked which animals. Tap the mistake.
steps.feedback: They read it literally. A metaphor is never meant to be true.

steps.narration: Tap the simile: 'the road was a ribbon' or 'the road wound like a ribbon'.

questions.retryFeedback: Starting again usually loses the good parts too.

She had tried to fix each sentence as she wrote, and finished nothing.

content.subject: Writing
content.title: Exactly What He Said
content.objective: Quotation marks are a promise about the words themselves.
content.parentNote: Write down one thing someone says today, word for word.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: The school paper asked Yusuf to report what the caretaker had said.
The caretaker said: "The old gate is heavy, but it still shuts."
Yusuf wrote: "The old gate is heavy and broken." It read better, he thought.
