content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Your First Python: print()
content.objective: Write and run a one-line Python program.
content.accessibility: Code editor supports screen readers and adjustable font size; output is read aloud on request.

assets.desc: Kid-friendly Python editor with Run button

steps.narration: Type:  print("Hello, world!")  then press Run.
steps.feedback: Output box shows: Hello, world!

steps.narration: Change the words inside the quotes to your own message and Run again.
steps.feedback: Your message prints. You're a programmer.

steps.narration: Challenge: print your name and your age on two lines.
steps.feedback: Two print() lines make two lines of output.

steps.narration: Quotation marks tell Python where your message starts and stops.
steps.feedback: Leave one off and the program stops before it prints anything.

steps.narration: A program printed nothing at all. Tap the most likely cause.
steps.feedback: A missing quotation mark, or a misspelled command. Both are silent.

steps.narration: Tap what the computer does with the words inside the quotation marks.
steps.feedback: Prints them exactly, spaces and all. It never tidies them up for you.

steps.narration: Write a one-line program that prints a message to someone at home.
steps.feedback: One line is a real program. Everything else is more lines.

steps.narration: Every program you will ever write is built out of steps this small.
steps.feedback: A big program is not a clever line. It is many small ones in order.

recap.prompt: Which Python command shows text on the screen?
Two print() lines produce how many lines of output?

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Variables Store Values
content.objective: Use a variable to store and reuse a value.
content.accessibility: Editor supports screen readers and adjustable font; output read on request.

assets.desc: A labeled box holding a value, like a container

steps.narration: Type:  name = "Sam"   then   print(name)   and Run.
steps.feedback: Output: Sam. The variable 'name' holds your text.

steps.narration: Change the value: name = "Ada" and Run again.
steps.feedback: Output: Ada. One variable, many values!

steps.narration: Make a variable  age = 10  and print it.
steps.feedback: Variables let programs remember things.

steps.narration: A variable is a name pointing at a value. The name stays; the value moves.
steps.feedback: That is why you can print a name and get whatever it holds today.

steps.narration: A program sets total to 5, then sets total to total plus 7. What does it print?
steps.feedback: 12. It read its own value, added, then stored the answer back.

steps.narration: Someone set total to 5, then to 9, and expected 14. Tap the mistake.
steps.feedback: Assigning replaces. The 5 was gone the moment the 9 arrived.

steps.narration: Tap why a program prints a name without any quotation marks around it.
steps.feedback: Quotes mean the letters themselves; no quotes means look inside the box.

steps.narration: Name three values a game keeps in variables while you play it.
steps.feedback: Score, lives, level. Every number on screen that changes is one.

recap.prompt: After name = "Ada", what does printing name show?
Can one variable hold different values at different times?

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Loops with for
content.objective: Repeat actions using a for loop.
content.accessibility: Indentation is announced; output read aloud on request.

assets.desc: Arrow looping back to repeat a step

steps.narration: Type:  for i in range(3):  then indented  print("Hi")  and Run.
steps.feedback: Hi prints three times. The loop repeats.

steps.narration: Change range(3) to range(5) and Run.
steps.feedback: Now it prints five times. Loops save typing.

steps.narration: Loop to print the numbers 1, 2, 3.
steps.feedback: Loops are a programmer's superpower.

steps.narration: The indented lines under a loop are the part that repeats.
steps.feedback: Indentation is not decoration in Python. It is the grammar.

steps.narration: A loop runs over range(5). How many times does the indented line run?
steps.feedback: 5. range(5) counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five turns.

steps.narration: A line printed once instead of five times. Tap the likely reason.
steps.feedback: It was not indented, so it sat outside the loop and ran after it.

steps.narration: A loop over range(3) prints two lines each time. How many lines in total?
steps.feedback: 6. Three turns, two lines a turn.

steps.narration: Count something repetitive in your day and say it as a loop out loud.
steps.feedback: Twelve stairs, twenty-eight teeth. Loops are how you say them briefly.

recap.prompt: for i in range(5) repeats how many times?
Why use a for loop?
options: It saves typing the same line

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: If / Else Decisions
content.objective: Make a program choose between two paths.
content.accessibility: Logic is described step by step; output read aloud.

assets.desc: A path splitting into two based on a question

steps.narration: Type:  if score >= 10:  print("You win!")  else:  print("Try again").  Set score = 12 and Run.
steps.feedback: Output: You win! The condition was true.

steps.narration: Change score to 4 and Run.
steps.feedback: Output: Try again. The else path ran.

steps.narration: Conditions let programs react differently to different data.
steps.feedback: Now your code can decide.

steps.narration: A condition is checked once, and only one branch runs. Never both.
steps.feedback: The else branch is skipped entirely, not run quietly in the background.

steps.narration: A score of 10 is tested against 'score is 10 or more'. Tap which branch runs.
steps.feedback: The first. 'Or more' includes exactly ten, which is the usual trap.

steps.narration: Someone wrote a rule with no else branch. Tap what happens on a false test.
steps.feedback: Nothing at all — which is sometimes right, and sometimes the whole bug.

steps.narration: Tap the test a program could actually run: 'the door is locked' or 'the film is good'.
steps.feedback: The lock. A condition needs a fact, and good cannot be measured.

steps.narration: Say a rule from your home as if-else, including the false case.
steps.feedback: Most people only ever say the 'if' half. The else is where arguments start.

recap.prompt: score = 12 and the rule is score >= 10. Which path runs?
What runs when the condition is false?

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Find and Fix the Bug
content.objective: Debug a short program that has an error.
content.parentNote: Praise the persistence it takes to track down a bug.
content.accessibility: Error messages are read aloud; the editor highlights the flagged line.

assets.desc: A magnifying glass over a line of code

steps.narration: This code should print 'Hello' but prints nothing. The line  prnt("Hello")  has a typo. Tap the bug.
steps.feedback: Found it. 'prnt' should be 'print'.

steps.narration: Fix it to  print("Hello")  and Run.
steps.feedback: Output: Hello. Debugged!

steps.narration: Good programmers read errors calmly and fix one thing at a time.
steps.feedback: Patience is a coding skill.

steps.narration: An error message is not a telling-off. It is the computer showing its working.
steps.feedback: It usually names the line, and the line it names is usually right.

steps.narration: A misspelled command stops the program. Tap what the computer does with it.
steps.feedback: Reports it and stops. It cannot guess what you meant, and will not try.

steps.narration: Tap the best way to find a bug in a program twenty lines long.
steps.feedback: Run a few lines at a time and watch where it first goes wrong.

steps.narration: A program runs but prints the wrong number. Tap why that is harder to fix.
steps.feedback: Nothing reports it. A silent wrong answer is worse than a loud crash.

steps.narration: Next time something you built fails, read the message before changing anything.
steps.feedback: Most of debugging is reading carefully, not typing cleverly.

recap.prompt: prnt("Hello") does not work. What is wrong?
What is the best way to fix errors?

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Smart and Safe Online
content.objective: Protect privacy and judge if a source is trustworthy.
content.parentNote: Agree on what personal details should never be shared online.
content.accessibility: Choices are illustrated, labeled, and read aloud.

steps.narration: A strong password is long and mixes letters, numbers, and symbols. Tap the stronger password.
steps.feedback: Longer and mixed is harder to guess.

steps.narration: Never share your address or passwords with strangers online. Tap the safe choice.
steps.feedback: Keep private things private.

steps.narration: Before trusting a website, ask: who wrote it, and is it backed up elsewhere?
steps.feedback: Smart readers check their sources!

steps.narration: A long password beats a clever short one. Length is what makes guessing slow.
steps.feedback: Three unrelated words beat one word with letters swapped for numbers.

steps.narration: Tap the safer password: your dog's name, or three unrelated words joined up.
steps.feedback: The three words. A pet's name is on the internet already, in a photo caption.

steps.narration: A website has no author's name anywhere. Tap what that should do to your trust.
steps.feedback: Lower it. Somebody willing to be named is somebody who can be checked.

steps.narration: Tap the best way to check whether something online is true.
steps.feedback: Find it somewhere else that has no reason to copy the first one.

steps.narration: Check one thing you read online today against a second, separate source.
steps.feedback: Two sources that copied each other are still only one source.

recap.prompt: A strong password is long and mixes letters, numbers and…
Before trusting a website, what should you check?

content.title: What Will Python Print?
content.objective: Trace a tiny program's output.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: It was not indented, so it sat outside the loop

questions.prompt: What does  print(2 + 3)  show?
questions.correctFeedback: Python adds first, so it prints 5.
questions.retryFeedback: Python solves the math inside print(). Try again!

questions.prompt: What does  print("2" + "3")  show?

questions.retryFeedback: Quotes make it text, so it joins. Try again!

questions.prompt: A loop runs over range(5). How many times does the indented line run?
questions.correctFeedback: range(5) counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five turns.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the numbers it produces, not the last one.

questions.prompt: A line printed once instead of five times. What is the likely reason?

options.label: It was not indented, so it sat outside the loop

questions.correctFeedback: Indentation is not decoration in Python. It is the grammar.
questions.retryFeedback: Look at which lines line up under the loop.

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Trace the Loop
content.objective: Predict the output of a loop.
content.accessibility: Code read aloud on tap.

questions.prompt: How many times does this print?  for i in range(4):  print("hi")
questions.correctFeedback: range(4) repeats 4 times.
questions.retryFeedback: range(4) gives 0,1,2,3. That's 4 times. Try again!

questions.prompt: What does a variable do?
questions.correctFeedback: A variable stores a value you can reuse.
questions.retryFeedback: Think of a labeled box holding something. Try again!

questions.prompt: A program sets total to 5, then to total plus 7. What does it print?
questions.correctFeedback: It read its own value, added, then stored the answer back.
questions.retryFeedback: The variable is on both sides of that line for a reason.

questions.prompt: A misspelled command stops a program. What does the computer do?
questions.correctFeedback: It cannot guess, and would be dangerous if it tried.
questions.retryFeedback: An error message is the computer showing its working.

content.title: Stay Safe Online
content.objective: Choose safe online habits.
content.accessibility: Options read aloud.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest password?

questions.retryFeedback: Longer with letters, numbers, and symbols is best. Try again!

questions.prompt: A stranger online asks for your home address. What should you do?

options.label: Don't share it and tell a trusted adult

content.title: Read the Program
content.objective: Trace loops, variables and conditions without running them.
content.parentNote: Ask them to predict, then check. Predicting is the skill.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: A loop over range(3) prints two lines each turn. How many lines in total?
questions.correctFeedback: Three turns, two lines a turn.
questions.retryFeedback: Multiply the turns by the lines inside.

questions.prompt: total is 5, then total becomes total minus 2, twice. What is total?
questions.correctFeedback: Five, minus two, minus two again.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the step twice, not once.

questions.prompt: A score of 10 is tested against 'score is 10 or more'. Which branch runs?
questions.correctFeedback: 'Or more' includes exactly ten. That is the usual trap.
questions.retryFeedback: Read the words of the condition carefully.

questions.correctFeedback: A silent wrong answer is worse than a loud crash.
questions.retryFeedback: Errors that stop the program at least tell you where.

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: Ada and the Stuck Robot
content.objective: Debugging is reading your own instructions honestly.
content.parentNote: Ask what Ada did before she changed anything.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Ada's robot was supposed to walk to the door, but it kept spinning in circles.
'It's broken,' said her brother. Ada was not so sure.
She read the code line by line, running it a few steps at a time.
One step said 'turn' four times but never 'walk forward'. Tap to spot it.
The robot had done exactly what she wrote. It had never been broken.
Ada added 'walk forward' and ran it again. Bugs aren't scary. They're puzzles.

pages.narration: Ada's robot was supposed to walk to the door, but it kept spinning in circles.
'It's broken,' said her brother. Ada was not so sure.

content.subject: Digital Literacy & Coding
content.title: The Message That Was Not True
content.objective: Checking a source is a habit, not a suspicion.
content.parentNote: Check one thing you read online together this week.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: A message went round Kwame's class: the school would close on Friday.
Everyone had seen it, so everyone believed it. That felt like proof.
Kwame looked for the original. It had no author and no date.
He checked the school's own notice board. Friday was a normal day.
He told his class where he had looked, not just what he had found.

pages.narration: A message went round Kwame's class: the school would close on Friday.
Everyone had seen it, so everyone believed it. That felt like proof.
Kwame looked for the original. It had no author and no date.
Twenty people sharing one message is still only one message.
He checked the school's own notice board. Friday was a normal day.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Long Division, Step by Step
content.objective: Work through long division (Divide-Multiply-Subtract-Bring down).
content.accessibility: Each step can be replayed; an optional worked-example video has captions.

steps.narration: Solve 84 ÷ 4. Step 1. Divide: how many 4s in 8?
steps.feedback: 2. Write it above the 8.

steps.narration: Step 2. Multiply 2 × 4, Step 3. Subtract from 8.
steps.feedback: 8 - 8 = 0. Bring down the 4.

steps.narration: Step 4. Divide 4 ÷ 4, then finish.
steps.feedback: 1. So 84 ÷ 4 = 21. You used D-M-S-B.

steps.narration: Long division is four steps on repeat: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
steps.feedback: The loop ends when there is nothing left to bring down.

steps.narration: Work 96 ÷ 4. How many 4s go into 9?
steps.feedback: 2, with 1 left over. That leftover is what you carry across.

steps.narration: Bring down the 6 to make 16. How many 4s go into 16?
Someone forgot to bring the second digit down. Tap what their answer looks like.
steps.feedback: Far too small — a single digit where two belong.

steps.narration: Share a large number of something between four people, on paper.
steps.feedback: Long division is just sharing, written down carefully.

recap.prompt: Which step comes first in long division?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Multiply Two-Digit Numbers
content.objective: Multiply a two-digit number using place value.
content.accessibility: Each partial product is announced; a grid model can be toggled on.

steps.narration: 23 × 4. Break 23 into 20 + 3. Multiply each: 20×4=80, 3×4=12.
steps.feedback: Partial products: 80 and 12.

steps.narration: Add the partial products: 80 + 12 = ?
Try 31 × 5 the same way: (30×5) + (1×5).
steps.feedback: 150 + 5 = 155. Place value makes it easy.

steps.narration: Splitting a number by place value turns one hard sum into two easy ones.
steps.feedback: 23 × 4 is 20 × 4 and 3 × 4, and you already know both.

steps.narration: Split 41 × 3. What is 40 × 3?
steps.feedback: 120. Four threes, then the zero.

steps.narration: Now add the other part: 120 + (1 × 3).
steps.feedback: 123. Two easy sums instead of one hard one.

steps.narration: Someone worked 23 × 4 as 80 and stopped. Tap what they left out.
steps.feedback: The 3 × 4. Splitting only works if you add both parts back.

steps.narration: Work out the cost of 4 items at 23 coins each, in your head, by splitting.
steps.feedback: This is the trick people who are fast at mental maths are actually using.

recap.prompt: Breaking 23 into 20 + 3 to multiply each part gives you…

content.subject: Math
content.title: Equivalent Fractions
content.objective: Find fractions that name the same amount.
content.accessibility: Fraction bars have labels and high-contrast fills; values read aloud.

steps.narration: 1/2 of a bar is shaded. Split each half again. Now it's 2/4. Same amount!
Multiply top and bottom by the same number: 1/2 × 2/2 = 2/4.
steps.feedback: That's the rule for equal fractions.

steps.narration: Make a fraction equal to 1/3 by multiplying by 3/3.
Multiplying top and bottom by the same number changes the name, not the amount.
steps.feedback: You are cutting the same cake into more, smaller pieces.

steps.narration: 1/3 is multiplied top and bottom by 3. What is the new bottom number?
steps.feedback: 9. And the top becomes 3, giving 3/9 — the same amount.

steps.narration: Someone turned 1/2 into 2/3 by adding one to each part. Tap the error.
steps.feedback: Adding changes the value. Only multiplying keeps it the same.

steps.narration: Tap the fraction equal to 1/2: 3/6, 2/5, or 4/9.
steps.feedback: 3/6. The bottom is exactly twice the top, which is what a half means.

steps.narration: Fold a strip of paper in half, then in half again, and name what you see.
steps.feedback: One half and two quarters are the same fold, counted differently.

recap.prompt: Which fraction names the same amount as 1/2?
To make an equal fraction, multiply the top and bottom by…

content.subject: Math
content.title: Add Fractions (Same Bottom)
content.objective: Add and subtract fractions with like denominators.
content.accessibility: Numerator and denominator are announced separately.

assets.desc: Two fifths added to one fifth

steps.narration: 1/5 + 2/5. The bottoms match, so add the tops: 1 + 2 = 3.
The denominator stays the same. It tells the size of each piece.
steps.feedback: Only the top changes.
3/6. Great. Same bottom, subtract the tops!

steps.narration: When the bottoms match, add the tops. The bottom is the size of the piece.
steps.feedback: Adding bottoms too would change the size of every piece mid-sum.

steps.narration: Add 2/7 and 3/7. What is the new top number?
steps.feedback: 5. Five sevenths — the sevenths never changed.

steps.narration: Now work 4/6 minus 1/6. What is the top number of the answer?
steps.feedback: 3. Subtracting works exactly the same way.

steps.narration: Someone added 1/4 and 2/4 and wrote 3/8. Tap what they did wrong.
steps.feedback: They added the bottoms too. The pieces cannot shrink halfway through.

steps.narration: Cut a fruit into six and add the pieces back together out loud.
steps.feedback: Six sixths is one whole, and hearing yourself say it makes it stick.

recap.prompt: When you add fractions with the same bottom, what changes?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Tenths and Hundredths
content.objective: Read decimals to the hundredths place.
content.accessibility: Place-value chart can be toggled; decimals read in words.

steps.narration: 0.7 means 7 tenths. 7 out of 10 parts. Tap the 7th mark.
steps.feedback: 0.7 = seven tenths.

steps.narration: 0.25 means 25 hundredths. Two digits after the dot = hundredths.
steps.feedback: 0.25 = twenty-five hundredths.

steps.narration: Which is bigger, 0.5 or 0.45? Line up the dots.
steps.feedback: 0.5 is bigger. 5 tenths beats 4 tenths.

steps.narration: The digits after the dot are tenths, then hundredths — the same pattern, smaller.
steps.feedback: Place value does not stop at the dot. It just keeps dividing by ten.

steps.narration: Tap the larger number: 0.6 or 0.59.
steps.feedback: 0.6, because six tenths beats five tenths. Length of the number means nothing.

steps.narration: Someone said 0.59 is bigger because it has more digits. Tap the mistake.
steps.feedback: Compare from the left, one place at a time, as you would with whole numbers.

steps.narration: Tap what 0.25 means as a fraction of one whole.
steps.feedback: Twenty-five hundredths, which is also one quarter.

steps.narration: Find two prices in a shop and say which is larger before you look at the labels twice.
steps.feedback: Money is decimals, and decimals are where most people slip.

recap.prompt: How many tenths does 0.7 mean?
Which is bigger, 0.5 or 0.45?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Area and Perimeter
content.objective: Find area and perimeter of rectangles.
content.accessibility: Grid squares are countable with audio; formulas shown and spoken.

assets.desc: Labeled 5 by 3 rectangle on a grid

steps.narration: A rectangle is 5 long and 3 wide. Perimeter = add all sides: 5+3+5+3.
steps.feedback: Perimeter = 16 units.

steps.narration: Area = length × width = 5 × 3.
steps.feedback: Area = 15 square units.

steps.narration: Try a 6 × 2 rectangle: find both.
steps.feedback: Perimeter 16, area 12. You've got it.

steps.narration: Perimeter is the walk around the edge. Area is the floor inside it.
steps.feedback: They answer different questions: fencing a garden, or turfing it.

steps.narration: A rectangle is 6 long and 2 wide. What is its area?
steps.feedback: 12 square units. Length times width, always.

steps.narration: Same rectangle, 6 by 2. What is its perimeter?
steps.feedback: 16. Six plus two plus six plus two — all four sides.

steps.narration: Someone gave an area in metres, not square metres. Tap why that is wrong.
steps.feedback: Area covers a surface, so its unit is squared. Perimeter is a length.

steps.narration: Measure a table and work out both. One tells you the cloth, the other the trim.
steps.feedback: Every builder uses both, and never confuses them.

recap.prompt: A rectangle is 5 long and 3 wide. What is its perimeter?
What is the area of that rectangle?

content.subject: Math
content.title: Multiply It
content.objective: Solve a two-digit multiplication.
content.accessibility: Options are large and screen-reader labeled.

questions.prompt: What is 23 × 4?
questions.correctFeedback: You split it into parts. (20×4) + (3×4) = 80 + 12 = 92.
questions.retryFeedback: Break 23 into 20 + 3, multiply each, then add. Try again!

questions.prompt: What is 12 × 6?
questions.retryFeedback: Try (10×6) + (2×6). Try again!

questions.prompt: What is 96 divided by 4?
questions.correctFeedback: Two into the nine, carry the one, then four into sixteen.
questions.retryFeedback: Do not forget to bring the second digit down.

questions.prompt: What is 41 × 3, worked out by splitting 41 into 40 and 1?
questions.correctFeedback: 120 and 3. Splitting only works if you add both parts back.
questions.retryFeedback: One of the two parts has been left behind.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Fraction Sense
content.objective: Identify equivalent fractions and sums.
content.accessibility: Fractions read as 'one half', etc.

questions.prompt: Which fraction equals 1/2?
questions.correctFeedback: 3/6 is the same as 1/2.
questions.retryFeedback: Does the top fit into the bottom exactly twice? Try again!

questions.prompt: What is 1/4 + 2/4?
questions.correctFeedback: Same bottom, add the tops. 3/4.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep the denominator, add the numerators. Try again!

questions.prompt: Add 2/7 and 3/7. What is the answer?
questions.correctFeedback: The bottoms match, so add the tops. The sevenths never changed.
questions.retryFeedback: Adding the bottoms would shrink the pieces halfway through.

questions.prompt: 1/3 is multiplied top and bottom by 3. What do you get?
questions.correctFeedback: The same amount with a new name — the cake is cut into more pieces.
questions.retryFeedback: Adding one to each part would change the value, not the name.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Decimals and Area
content.objective: Compare decimals and compute area.
content.accessibility: Numbers and units read aloud.

questions.prompt: Which is larger: 0.6 or 0.59?
questions.correctFeedback: 0.6 is six tenths, larger than 0.59.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare tenths first. Try again!

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 4 by 3. What is its area?
questions.correctFeedback: 4 × 3 = 12 square units.
questions.retryFeedback: Area is length × width. Try again!

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 6 long and 2 wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.correctFeedback: All four sides: six, two, six, two. Twelve is the area, not the walk round.
questions.retryFeedback: Perimeter is the walk around the edge.

questions.prompt: What does 0.25 mean as a fraction of one whole?
questions.correctFeedback: Two digits after the dot means hundredths.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the places after the dot.

content.subject: Math
content.title: Divide, Split and Measure
content.objective: Apply long division, place value, fractions and area together.
content.parentNote: The area question is worth doing on a real table.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: What is 84 divided by 4?
questions.correctFeedback: Two into eight, then one into four. No remainder.
questions.retryFeedback: Work the digits left to right, one at a time.

questions.prompt: Which fraction equals 1/2?
questions.correctFeedback: The bottom is exactly twice the top, which is what a half means.
questions.retryFeedback: Check whether doubling the top gives you the bottom.

questions.prompt: Which is larger: 0.6 or 0.59?
questions.correctFeedback: Six tenths beats five tenths. Length of the number means nothing.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare from the left, one place at a time.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 4 by 3. What is its area?
questions.correctFeedback: Length times width. Fourteen is the perimeter, not the area.
questions.retryFeedback: Area covers the inside; perimeter walks the edge.

content.subject: Math
content.title: The Bake Sale Budget
content.objective: Multiplication, costs and profit in one real problem.
content.parentNote: Work out the profit together before the last page.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Lina's class wants to raise money. Each tray costs 8 coins and holds 12 muffins.
They make 4 trays. How many muffins is that? Tap to work out 4 × 12.
Split it: 4 × 10 is 40, and 4 × 2 is 8. Forty-eight muffins.
At 2 coins each, that is 96 coins in. But the trays cost 32 coins out.
96 minus 32 leaves 64. Profit is only ever what is left after costs.

pages.narration: Lina's class wants to raise money. Each tray costs 8 coins and holds 12 muffins.
They make 4 trays. How many muffins is that? Tap to work out 4 × 12.
Split it: 4 × 10 is 40, and 4 × 2 is 8. Forty-eight muffins.
At 2 coins each, that is 96 coins in. But the trays cost 32 coins out.
96 minus 32 leaves 64. Profit is only ever what is left after costs.
64 coins for the class trip. Teamwork and maths, together.

content.subject: Math
content.title: The Rug That Did Not Fit
content.objective: Area and perimeter answer different questions.
content.parentNote: Measure a room together and work out both numbers.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Mr Oyelaran measured his room and wrote down one number: 16.
He bought a rug of 16 and it covered barely a quarter of the floor.
What a rug needs is the area: six times two, which is twelve.
He measured again, twice, and wrote down both. The second rug fitted.

pages.narration: Mr Oyelaran measured his room and wrote down one number: 16.
He bought a rug of 16 and it covered barely a quarter of the floor.
The 16 was his perimeter — the walk around the edge, six by two.
What a rug needs is the area: six times two, which is twelve.
Perimeter buys skirting board. Area buys carpet. They are never the same job.
He measured again, twice, and wrote down both. The second rug fitted.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Similes and Metaphors
content.objective: Tell the difference between a simile and a metaphor.
content.accessibility: Examples are read aloud; key comparison words are highlighted.

assets.desc: Illustration of a lion and a smiling sun

steps.narration: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as': 'brave as a lion'. Tap the simile.
steps.feedback: 'As' signals a simile.

steps.narration: A metaphor says one thing is another: 'the classroom was a zoo'. Tap the metaphor.
steps.feedback: No 'like' or 'as'. It simply is.

steps.narration: Is 'her smile was sunshine' a simile or metaphor?
steps.feedback: A metaphor. It says the smile is sunshine.

steps.narration: Both compare a voice to thunder. A simile admits it with 'like'; a metaphor does not.
steps.feedback: A metaphor is stronger because it does not ask permission first.

steps.narration: 'The stars were diamonds in the sky.' Tap which kind of comparison this is.
steps.feedback: A metaphor. It says they were, not that they were like.

steps.narration: 'He runs like the wind.' Tap which kind this is.
steps.feedback: A simile. One small word does all the marking.

steps.narration: Someone read 'the classroom was a zoo' and asked which animals. Tap the mistake.
steps.feedback: Read literally. A metaphor is never meant to be true, only vivid.

steps.narration: Describe the weather today twice: once as a simile, once as a metaphor.
steps.feedback: Rain like nails, or a sky that is a grey blanket. Both work.

recap.prompt: 'Brave as a lion' is which kind of comparison?
'Her smile was sunshine' is which kind?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Idioms
content.objective: Understand that idioms have a meaning beyond the words.
content.parentNote: Share an idiom from your family's language and what it really means.
content.accessibility: Literal and figurative meanings are shown side by side and read aloud.

assets.desc: Playful art of an easy task labeled 'a piece of cake'

steps.narration: 'It's raining cats and dogs' doesn't mean animals fall! It means raining hard. Tap the real meaning.
steps.feedback: Idioms mean something figurative.

steps.narration: 'Break a leg' means 'good luck'. Tap the kind meaning.
steps.feedback: Right, not a real wish to get hurt.

steps.narration: What might 'a piece of cake' mean?
steps.feedback: Something very easy. Idioms are fun once you learn them.

steps.narration: An idiom means something its words never say. You cannot work it out.
steps.feedback: That is why they are so hard in a language you are learning.

steps.narration: 'A piece of cake' is said about a task. Tap what it means.
steps.feedback: Very easy. Nothing to do with cake, and no clue in the words.

steps.narration: An actor is about to walk on stage. Tap what 'break a leg' means.
steps.feedback: Good luck. Its history is odd, and knowing it is the only way to know it.

steps.narration: Someone learning English took 'raining cats and dogs' literally. Tap what would help.
steps.feedback: Someone telling them. Idioms have to be learned, not reasoned out.

steps.narration: Ask a grown-up for an idiom in another language you both know.
steps.feedback: Every language has them, and none of them translate.

recap.prompt: 'It's raining cats and dogs' means…
'A piece of cake' means something is…

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Finding the Theme
content.objective: Identify the central message or lesson of a story.
content.accessibility: Story summaries are read aloud; theme options are clearly labeled.

steps.narration: A theme is the big lesson, like 'never give up' or 'kindness matters'. It's not just what happens.
steps.feedback: Theme = the message behind the story.

steps.narration: In a tale where a slow tortoise wins by trying hard, the theme is...?
steps.feedback: 'Steady effort wins'. That's the theme.

steps.narration: Ask: what did the character learn? That points to the theme.
steps.feedback: Smart reading strategy!

steps.narration: The plot is what happened. The theme is what it was about.
steps.feedback: Two stories with completely different events can share one theme.

steps.narration: A slow tortoise beats a fast hare by never stopping. Tap the theme.
steps.feedback: Persistence beats speed. 'A tortoise won a race' is the plot, not the theme.

steps.narration: Tap the question that leads you to a story's theme.
steps.feedback: What did the character learn? Themes are almost always about change.

steps.narration: Someone said the theme was 'a girl shared her lunch'. Tap why that is the plot.
steps.feedback: It names an event. A theme would be 'kindness builds friendship'.

steps.narration: Name the theme of the last film you watched in four words or fewer.
steps.feedback: If you find yourself telling the plot, you have not found it yet.

recap.prompt: What is a theme?
options: The big lesson of a story

recap.prompt: A slow tortoise wins by trying hard. What is the theme?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Point of View
content.objective: Tell first-person from third-person narration.
content.accessibility: Pronouns are highlighted and announced.

steps.narration: First person uses 'I' and 'we'. The narrator is in the story. Tap the first-person line.
steps.feedback: 'I ran home' is first person.

steps.narration: Third person uses 'he', 'she', 'they'. A narrator outside the story. Tap it.
steps.feedback: Right. 'She ran home' is third person.

steps.narration: Who is telling the story changes how we see it.
steps.feedback: Great thinking!
steps.prompt: What changes how we see it?

steps.narration: Point of view decides what the reader knows: whose eyes the room is seen through.
steps.feedback: A first-person narrator cannot tell you what anyone else is thinking.

steps.narration: 'I couldn't believe what I saw.' Tap the point of view.
steps.feedback: First person. The narrator is inside the story, seeing part of it.

steps.narration: 'They opened the mysterious door.' Tap the point of view.
steps.feedback: Third person. The narrator watches from outside.

steps.narration: A dark house at midnight, told by the frightened child inside it. Tap what changes.
steps.feedback: You feel it instead of watching it, and you know less than they do not.

steps.narration: Retell one thing from your day in third person, as if you were watching.
steps.feedback: It sounds stranger than you expect, and that is the point.

recap.prompt: 'I ran home' is told in which point of view?
'She ran home' is told in which point of view?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Summarize a Passage
content.objective: Retell the key points in a short summary.
content.accessibility: Passage is read aloud; key sentences can be highlighted.

assets.desc: A long paragraph shrinking into three key points

steps.narration: A summary keeps only the most important ideas. Who, what, and why. Skip tiny details.
steps.feedback: A summary is short and focused.

steps.narration: Read a paragraph about a rescue dog. Tap the sentence that is just a small detail.
steps.feedback: The color of the collar isn't a key point.

steps.narration: Now keep the main events in order to build your summary.
steps.feedback: Clear and complete. Well done!
steps.prompt: How do events go in a summary?

steps.narration: A summary keeps who, what and why, and lets everything else go.
steps.feedback: If it is nearly as long as the original, it is a retelling, not a summary.

steps.narration: A passage tells how a rescue dog was found, trained and rehomed. Tap the best summary.
steps.feedback: 'A stray dog was rescued and found a new home.' Three stages, one sentence.

steps.narration: From the same passage, tap the detail a summary should drop.
steps.feedback: The colour of its collar. True, but it changes nothing about the story.

steps.narration: Someone's summary added what they thought of the story. Tap why that is wrong.
steps.feedback: A summary reports the author, not the reader. Opinions belong elsewhere.

steps.narration: Summarise a whole book to somebody in three sentences.
steps.feedback: Three is where the skill lives. Ten is just talking.

recap.prompt: A summary keeps the most important ideas and skips…
How do events go in a summary?

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Read Between the Lines
content.objective: Make an inference using text clues.
content.accessibility: Clue words are highlighted; prompts accept typed or spoken answers.

assets.desc: A child bundled in winter clothes

steps.narration: 'Mateo zipped his coat and stamped his boots in the snow.' Is it warm or cold?
steps.feedback: Cold. The coat, the boots and the snow are the clues.

steps.narration: An inference is a smart guess from evidence in the text.
steps.feedback: You combined clues with what you know.

steps.narration: 'Her stomach growled as she eyed the clock.' What can you infer?
steps.feedback: She's hungry and waiting. Good inference!

steps.narration: An inference is supported by the text but never stated in it.
steps.feedback: It has to come from the clues, not from what you already assume.

steps.narration: 'Mateo zipped his coat and stamped his boots in the snow.' Tap what you infer.
steps.feedback: It is cold. Nothing in the sentence says so — the coat and boots do.

steps.narration: 'Her stomach growled as she eyed the clock.' Tap the best inference.
steps.feedback: She is hungry and waiting for a meal. Two clues, one conclusion.

steps.narration: From that sentence someone inferred she was bored. Tap why that goes too far.
steps.feedback: The clock fits hunger just as well. Pick the reading that uses both clues.

steps.narration: Watch somebody come through a door and infer one thing about their day.
steps.feedback: Then ask, and find out whether your clues were any good.

recap.prompt: 'Mateo zipped his coat and stamped his boots in the snow.' What can you infer about the weather?
An inference is…

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Simile or Metaphor?
content.objective: Classify figurative language.
content.accessibility: Sentences read aloud on tap.

questions.prompt: 'The stars were diamonds in the sky.' This is a...
questions.correctFeedback: It says stars are diamonds, so it's a metaphor.
questions.retryFeedback: Does it use 'like' or 'as'? If not, it's a metaphor. Try again!

questions.prompt: 'He runs like the wind.' This is a...
questions.correctFeedback: 'Like' makes it a simile.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for 'like' or 'as'. Try again!

questions.prompt: Someone read 'the classroom was a zoo' and asked which animals. What went wrong?
questions.correctFeedback: A metaphor is never meant to be true, only vivid.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask what feeling the comparison is reaching for.

questions.prompt: What does the idiom 'a piece of cake' mean?
questions.correctFeedback: Nothing to do with cake, and no clue in the words themselves.
questions.retryFeedback: Idioms have to be learned, not reasoned out.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: What's the Theme?
content.objective: Identify the message of a short story.
content.accessibility: Story summary read aloud.

assets.desc: A stray dog was rescued and found a new home

questions.prompt: A girl shares her lunch with a new student and they become friends. What is the theme?
questions.correctFeedback: The lesson is that kindness builds friendship.
questions.retryFeedback: The theme is the big lesson, not a small detail. Try again!

questions.prompt: A slow tortoise beats a fast hare by never stopping. What is the theme?
questions.correctFeedback: The second one is the plot. A theme is the lesson underneath it.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask what the character learned.

questions.prompt: A passage tells how a rescue dog was found, trained and rehomed. Best summary?

options.label: A stray dog was rescued and found a new home
The dog wore a red collar

questions.correctFeedback: Three stages in one sentence. The collar is a detail that changes nothing.
questions.retryFeedback: A summary keeps who, what and why.

questions.prompt: 'Mateo zipped his coat and stamped his boots in the snow.' What can you infer?
questions.correctFeedback: Nothing in the sentence says so — the coat and the boots do.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the clues that are actually there.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Whose Point of View?
content.objective: Identify narration point of view.
content.accessibility: Pronouns announced.

assets.desc: She is hungry and waiting for a meal

questions.prompt: 'I couldn't believe what I saw.' What point of view is this?
questions.correctFeedback: 'I' means first person.
questions.retryFeedback: Who is speaking. Someone inside or outside the story? Try again!

questions.prompt: 'They opened the mysterious door.' What point of view?
questions.correctFeedback: 'They' means third person.
questions.retryFeedback: Look at the pronoun. Try again!

questions.prompt: A first-person narrator cannot tell you what?
questions.correctFeedback: They only know their own head. That limit is the whole effect.
questions.retryFeedback: Think about what one person can actually know.

questions.prompt: 'Her stomach growled as she eyed the clock.' What is the best inference?

options.label: She is hungry and waiting for a meal

questions.correctFeedback: Two clues, one conclusion. Boredom uses only half of them.
questions.retryFeedback: Pick the reading that uses both clues.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Beneath the Words
content.objective: Apply figurative language, idioms, theme and point of view.
content.parentNote: Ask which answer needed re-reading. That is where the learning is.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

questions.prompt: 'The stars were diamonds in the sky.' Simile or metaphor?
questions.correctFeedback: It says they were, not that they were like.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for 'like' or 'as'. There is neither here.

questions.prompt: What does 'break a leg' mean before a performance?
questions.correctFeedback: Its history is odd, and being told is the only way to know it.
questions.retryFeedback: Idioms cannot be worked out from their words.

questions.prompt: A girl shares her lunch with a new student and they become friends. The theme?
questions.correctFeedback: The other one is the plot. A theme is the lesson underneath.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask what the story is really about.

questions.prompt: 'I couldn't believe what I saw.' What point of view is this?
questions.correctFeedback: The narrator is inside the story, and can only see part of it.
questions.retryFeedback: Look at the pronouns doing the telling.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: The Bridge Builder
content.objective: Why an author includes something is a question worth asking.
content.parentNote: Ask why the grandfather's saying is in the story at all.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Ama studied the gap between the two cliffs. The village needed a way across.
She sketched, erased, and sketched again. Nothing held on paper.
She stopped rushing. The sketch that worked took three more days.
Why do you think the author tells us the grandfather's saying? Tap to share.

pages.narration: Ama studied the gap between the two cliffs. The village needed a way across.
The rains were coming, and she was the only engineer for a hundred miles.
She sketched, erased, and sketched again. Nothing held on paper.
'A bridge is just patience made of rope and wood,' her grandfather had said.
She stopped rushing. The sketch that worked took three more days.
Why do you think the author tells us the grandfather's saying? Tap to share.

content.subject: Reading
content.title: Two Ways to Tell It
content.objective: Point of view changes what a reader is allowed to know.
content.parentNote: Retell a family story from somebody else's point of view.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Nadia's class wrote about the same lost dog, and no two accounts matched.
Nadia wrote 'I heard him barking and my heart jumped.' You felt it with her.
Tom wrote 'They searched the park while the dog slept under a bench.'
His reader knew where the dog was the whole time, and worried differently.

pages.narration: Nadia's class wrote about the same lost dog, and no two accounts matched.
Nadia wrote 'I heard him barking and my heart jumped.' You felt it with her.
But she could not tell you what the dog's owner was thinking. She never knew.
Tom wrote 'They searched the park while the dog slept under a bench.'
His reader knew where the dog was the whole time, and worried differently.
Same dog, same park. Who is telling it decides what you are allowed to know.

content.subject: Science
content.title: Electricity and Circuits
content.objective: Build a simple circuit to light a bulb.
content.accessibility: Circuit state is announced aloud; works with switch controls.

steps.narration: Connect the battery, wire, and bulb to make a loop.
steps.feedback: The bulb lights. A complete circuit lets current flow.

steps.narration: Now open a gap in the wire.
steps.feedback: The light goes out. A broken circuit stops the flow.

steps.narration: Electricity only flows round a complete loop. One gap stops everything.
steps.feedback: A switch is nothing more than a gap you can open and close on purpose.

steps.narration: What happens to the bulb when you cut the wire anywhere in the loop?
steps.feedback: It goes out. Where the gap is does not matter — only that there is one.

steps.narration: Which material will let the circuit work if you put it in the gap?
steps.feedback: Metal. Wood, plastic and rubber all stop it, which is why wires wear them.

steps.narration: The bulb is in but the loop stays dark. What is missing?
steps.feedback: The push. A loop with no battery is a road with nothing travelling on it.

steps.narration: Why is a switch put in the wire rather than beside it?
steps.feedback: It has to be part of the loop to break it. Beside it, it does nothing.

steps.narration: Find three switches at home and say where the gap is in each.
steps.feedback: Every one of them is breaking a loop you cannot see.

recap.prompt: What makes the bulb light up?
What happens when you open a gap in the wire?

content.subject: Science
content.title: The Solar System
content.objective: Identify the planets orbiting the Sun.
content.accessibility: Planets are labeled, color-coded, and read aloud; relative sizes described.

assets.desc: The eight planets orbiting the Sun

steps.narration: Eight planets orbit the Sun. The four closest are rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars. Tap Earth.
steps.feedback: Earth. Our home, the third planet.

steps.narration: The four outer planets are giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Tap Saturn, the ringed one.
steps.feedback: Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock.

steps.narration: A year is one trip around the Sun. Farther planets take longer.
steps.feedback: Neptune's year is 165 Earth years.

steps.narration: The four inner planets are rock; the four outer ones are gas and ice.
steps.feedback: That split is about how hot it was where each one formed.

steps.narration: How many planets lie between Earth and the Sun?
steps.feedback: 2. Mercury and Venus, in that order.

steps.narration: Why is a year on Neptune far longer than a year on Earth?
steps.feedback: Its orbit is enormous, and a year is one lap round the Sun.

steps.narration: Someone said the Sun goes round the Earth. What do we actually observe?
steps.feedback: The Earth spins, which makes the Sun appear to cross the sky.

steps.narration: Look for a planet tonight. Venus and Jupiter are the bright ones that do not twinkle.
steps.feedback: Twinkling is what starlight does after crossing our air. Planets are too close.

recap.prompt: Which planet has the famous rings?
Planets farther from the Sun take how long for one year?

content.subject: Science
content.title: Forms of Energy
content.objective: Recognize light, heat, sound, and motion energy.
content.accessibility: Each energy type has an icon, a sound sample, and a spoken label.

assets.desc: Lamp, drum, ball, and fire showing energy types

steps.narration: A lamp gives light energy. Tap the lamp.
steps.feedback: Light lets us see.

steps.narration: A drum makes sound energy when it vibrates. Tap the drum.
steps.feedback: Sound is energy we hear.

steps.narration: A rolling ball has motion energy; a fire gives heat. Energy can change form.
steps.feedback: Energy is never lost. It transforms.

steps.narration: A lamp, a drum, a rolling ball: energy is never made or lost, only changed in form.
steps.feedback: A torch turns chemical energy into light, and some of it into heat.

steps.narration: A guitar string vibrates. What kind of energy is it making?
steps.feedback: Sound. Vibration is what sound is, all the way to your ear.

steps.narration: What does a rolling ball's motion energy become when it stops?
steps.feedback: Heat, in the ground and the air. It went somewhere; it did not vanish.

steps.narration: Someone said a lamp creates light out of nothing. What is wrong?
steps.feedback: It converts electricity. Trace any energy back and it came from somewhere.

steps.narration: Name three energy changes in your kitchen in the next ten minutes.
steps.feedback: A kettle, a radio, a hand rubbing another hand. All three at once.

recap.prompt: A lamp gives which form of energy?
A vibrating drum gives which form of energy?

content.subject: Science
content.title: Food Webs
content.objective: Trace energy through a food web.
content.accessibility: Arrows are described; nodes are labeled and read aloud.

assets.desc: A food web linking grass, insects, frog, and hawk

steps.narration: Producers (plants) make energy from sunlight. Drag the Sun to the grass.
steps.feedback: Producers start every food web.

steps.narration: A grasshopper eats grass; a frog eats the grasshopper. Connect them.
steps.feedback: Energy moves up the web.

steps.narration: A web has many connected chains. Remove one animal and others are affected.
steps.feedback: Everything in nature is linked.

steps.narration: A web is many chains sharing links. Most animals eat more than one thing.
steps.feedback: That sharing is exactly what makes a habitat able to take a shock.

steps.narration: What do producers use to make their own energy?
steps.feedback: Sunlight. Only plants can do it, and everything else eats to get some.

steps.narration: If all the grass disappeared, what happens to the grasshoppers?
steps.feedback: They have less food, and so does everything that eats them.

steps.narration: Why does removing one animal affect species that never eat it?
steps.feedback: Their food's food changed. Effects travel two or three links along.

steps.narration: Draw a food web for a garden: leaves, snails, birds and a cat.
steps.feedback: Four creatures make more links than you expect. Try removing one.

recap.prompt: What starts every food web?
Remove one animal from a web and the others are…

content.subject: Science
content.title: Changes of Matter
content.objective: Describe melting, freezing, and evaporating.
content.accessibility: State changes are animated with described captions and spoken steps.

assets.desc: Ice, water, and vapor with arrows

steps.narration: Heat melts a solid into a liquid: ice into water. Tap to melt the ice.
steps.feedback: Melting adds heat.

steps.narration: Cooling freezes a liquid back to solid: water into ice. Tap the water to freeze it.
steps.feedback: Freezing removes heat.

steps.narration: More heat evaporates liquid into gas: water into vapor. Same stuff, new form.
steps.feedback: Matter can change state and back again.

steps.narration: Ice, water and steam: melting and freezing change the state, never the substance.
steps.feedback: Weigh ice, melt it, weigh the water. Nothing has been gained or lost.

steps.narration: What do you add to turn a solid into a liquid?
steps.feedback: Heat. Take it away again and it freezes back, exactly as it was.

steps.narration: A puddle vanishes on a warm day. Where did the water go?
steps.feedback: Into the air as vapour. You cannot see it, but it is entirely still there.

steps.narration: Someone said melted ice is a different substance. What is the mistake?
steps.feedback: Same substance, different state. Only the arrangement changed.

steps.narration: Put a lid on a pan of hot water and watch where the drops form.
steps.feedback: Evaporation and condensation, in one saucepan, in one minute.

recap.prompt: Heating ice until it becomes water is called…
Cooling water until it becomes ice is called…

content.subject: Science
content.title: Think Like a Scientist
content.objective: Follow the steps of the scientific method.
content.parentNote: Try a simple home experiment and ask your child to predict the result first.
content.accessibility: Each step is labeled, sequential, and read aloud; data log accepts typed or spoken entries.

steps.narration: First ask a question: 'Which paper plane flies farthest?' Tap to begin.
steps.feedback: A good question starts science.

steps.narration: Make a hypothesis (a smart guess), then test it with a fair experiment.
steps.feedback: Change one thing at a time.

steps.narration: Record results and draw a conclusion. Tap to log your data.
steps.feedback: Observe, test, conclude. That's science.

steps.narration: A fair test changes one thing and holds everything else still.
steps.feedback: Change two and you will never know which one caused the result.

steps.narration: You test which paper plane flies furthest. What must stay the same?
steps.feedback: The throw, the paper, the spot you stand. Only the fold should differ.

steps.narration: Before you throw a single paper plane, what is a hypothesis?
steps.feedback: A prediction you are willing to be wrong about, written down first.

steps.narration: Your result disagrees with your hypothesis. What is the right response?
steps.feedback: Record it and say so. A wrong prediction is a finding, not a failure.

steps.narration: Run one fair test at home this week and write the result before you forget it.
steps.feedback: Which paper towel holds most water is a real experiment.

questions.correctFeedback: It states the main idea. The others are details.
questions.retryFeedback: The topic sentence states the big idea. Try again!

questions.correctFeedback: A new line for each speaker costs nothing and fixes it.
questions.retryFeedback: That is the whole reason the rule exists.

content.subject: Writing
content.title: The Speech Jamal Wrote
content.objective: An argument is a structure, not a strong feeling.
content.parentNote: Ask what changed between his first draft and his last.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Jamal's first draft was three pages of how much he loved the library.
His sister read it and asked one question: why should anyone else care?
So he cut it to one claim, three reasons and a closing line.
Each reason was something a listener could check, not something he felt.
He read it aloud four times and cut a sentence each time.
It ran ninety seconds, and the whole hall listened to all of it.

content.subject: Writing
content.title: The Blank Page
content.objective: A bad first draft is the only way to reach a good last one.
content.parentNote: Try the ten-minute rule together: write badly, no stopping.
content.accessibility: All narration is also shown as captions; playable audio-only.

assets.desc: Priya had to write a story by Friday, and it was already Wednesday.
She wrote a sentence, read it, decided it was bad, and deleted it.
Her teacher's rule: write badly for ten minutes and do not stop, ever.
The ten minutes gave her four terrible paragraphs and one good idea.
She revised the good idea for an hour. You cannot revise a blank page.

pages.narration: Priya had to write a story by Friday, and it was already Wednesday.
She wrote a sentence, read it, decided it was bad, and deleted it.
She did that eleven times. The page was still blank at bedtime.
Her teacher's rule: write badly for ten minutes and do not stop, ever.
The ten minutes gave her four terrible paragraphs and one good idea.
She revised the good idea for an hour. You cannot revise a blank page.
